name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q01 - Shortest wavelength electromagnetic wave among rays

questiontext.text: The E.M. wave with shortest wavelength among the following is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The electromagnetic spectrum, in order of decreasing frequency and increasing wavelength, comprises gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet rays, visible light, infrared rays, microwaves, and radio waves.

Step 2: Evaluation
The characteristic wavelength intervals for the given regions of the spectrum are approximately:
• Gamma-rays: \(\lambda < 10^{-11}\text{ m}\)
• X-rays: \(10^{-11}\text{ m}\) to \(10^{-8}\text{ m}\)
• Ultraviolet rays: \(10^{-8}\text{ m}\) to \(4 \times 10^{-7}\text{ m}\)
• Microwaves: \(10^{-3}\text{ m}\) to \(0.3\text{ m}\)

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Among the given electromagnetic waves, gamma-rays have the highest frequency and therefore the shortest wavelength.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q02 - Angular acceleration of wheel increasing speed

questiontext.text: The angular speed of the wheel of a vehicle is increased from \(360\text{ rpm}\) to \(1200\text{ rpm}\) in \(14\text{ seconds}\). Its angular acceleration is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial rotational frequency: \(N_1 = 360\text{ rpm}\)
Final rotational frequency: \(N_2 = 1200\text{ rpm}\)
Time interval: \(t = 14\text{ s}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Assume uniform angular acceleration \(\alpha\) over the given time duration.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The relationship between rotational frequency \(N\) (in \(\text{rpm}\)) and angular speed \(\omega\) (in \(\text{rad/s}\)) is:
\[\omega = \frac{2\pi N}{60}\]
The angular acceleration is given by the rotational kinematic equation:
\[\alpha = \frac{\omega_2 - \omega_1}{t}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Convert the initial and final rotational speeds into radians per second:
\[\omega_1 = \frac{2\pi \times 360}{60} = 12\pi\text{ rad/s}\]
\[\omega_2 = \frac{2\pi \times 1200}{60} = 40\pi\text{ rad/s}\]
Calculate the angular acceleration:
\[\alpha = \frac{40\pi - 12\pi}{14} = \frac{28\pi}{14} = 2\pi\text{ rad/s}^2\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The calculated value is positive, corresponding to acceleration, with proper units of \(\text{rad/s}^2\). The angular acceleration is \(2\pi\text{ rad/s}^2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q03 - Effect of gamma radiation emission on nucleus

questiontext.text: What happens to the mass number and atomic number of an element when it emits \(\gamma\)-radiation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Gamma (\(\gamma\)) decay occurs when an atomic nucleus in an excited state de-excites to a lower energy level or its ground state by emitting energy in the form of high-frequency electromagnetic radiation (gamma photons).

Step 2: Evaluation
A gamma photon has zero rest mass and zero electric charge. The nuclear transition is represented by:
\[{}^A_Z X^* \to {}^A_Z X + \gamma\]
where \(A\) is the mass number and \(Z\) is the atomic number of the parent nucleus.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Since no protons or neutrons are gained, lost, or converted, both the mass number and the atomic number remain unchanged.

answer.text: Mass number decreases by four and atomic number decreases by two.
Mass number and atomic number remain unchanged.
Mass number remains unchanged while atomic number decreases by one.
Mass number increases by four and atomic number increases by two.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q04 - Value of one minute of arc in radian

questiontext.text: The angle of \(1'\) (minute of arc) in radian is nearly equal to

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Given plane angle: \(1'\) (one minute of arc).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Standard conversion relations between degrees, arcminutes, and radians are:
• \(180^\circ = \pi\text{ rad}\)
• \(1^\circ = 60'\)

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[1^\circ = \frac{\pi}{180}\text{ rad}\]
\[1' = \left(\frac{1}{60}\right)^\circ = \frac{\pi}{180 \times 60}\text{ rad} = \frac{\pi}{10800}\text{ rad}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the numerical value of \(\pi \approx 3.1416\):
\[1' = \frac{3.1416}{10800}\text{ rad} \approx 2.9089 \times 10^{-4}\text{ rad} \approx 2.91 \times 10^{-4}\text{ rad}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking against typical arc subdivisions: \(1^\circ \approx 1.75 \times 10^{-2}\text{ rad}\), \(1' \approx 2.91 \times 10^{-4}\text{ rad}\), and \(1'' \approx 4.85 \times 10^{-6}\text{ rad}\). The value of \(1'\) is \(2.91 \times 10^{-4}\text{ rad}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q05 - Induced electromotive force in a coil

questiontext.text:
The magnetic flux linked with a coil (in \(\text{Wb}\)) is given by the equation

\[\phi = 5t^2 + 3t + 16\]

The magnitude of induced emf in the coil at the fourth second will be

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Magnetic flux as a function of time: \(\phi(t) = 5t^2 + 3t + 16\) (in \(\text{Wb}\))
Time instant: \(t = 4\text{ s}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
By Faraday's law of induction, the induced electromotive force opposes the change in magnetic flux. Only the magnitude of the induced emf is required.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The magnitude of induced electromotive force is given by:
\[|e| = \left|\frac{d\phi}{dt}\right|\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Differentiate \(\phi\) with respect to time \(t\):
\[\frac{d\phi}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}(5t^2 + 3t + 16) = 10t + 3\]
Substitute \(t = 4\text{ s}\):
\[|e| = 10(4) + 3 = 40 + 3 = 43\text{ V}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The units are consistently \(\text{Wb/s} = \text{V}\). The magnitude of the induced electromotive force at the fourth second is \(43\text{ V}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q06 - Electric field on equatorial plane of dipole

questiontext.text: The electric field at a point on the equatorial plane at a distance \(r\) from the centre of a dipole having dipole moment \(\vec{p}\) is given by (\(r \gg\) separation of two charges forming the dipole, \(\varepsilon_0\) - permittivity of free space)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An electric dipole consists of two equal and opposite charges \(-q\) and \(+q\) separated by a distance \(2a\). The electric dipole moment vector \(\vec{p}\) is directed from the negative charge to the positive charge along the dipole axis.

Step 2: Evaluation
On the equatorial line (the perpendicular bisector of the dipole), the electric field components perpendicular to the dipole axis cancel each other due to symmetry, while the parallel components add up in the direction opposite to the dipole moment vector \(\vec{p}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For a short dipole where \(r \gg 2a\), the electric field at distance \(r\) is given in vector form by:
\[\vec{E} = -\frac{\vec{p}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^3}\]
The negative sign explicitly indicates that the electric field on the equatorial plane points in the direction opposite to the dipole moment vector.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The electric field on the equatorial plane is \(\vec{E} = -\frac{\vec{p}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^3}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q07 - Measurement of plano convex lens using spherometer

questiontext.text: A plano-convex lens of unknown material and unknown focal length is given. With the help of a spherometer we can measure the

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A spherometer is a precise mechanical instrument used to measure the sagitta (height of curvature, \(h\)) of spherical surfaces such as lenses and mirrors.

Step 2: Evaluation
Using the distance between the legs of the spherometer \(a\) and the sagitta \(h\), the radius of curvature \(R\) of the spherical surface is obtained directly from the geometric formula:
\[R = \frac{a^2}{6h} + \frac{h}{2}\]

Step 3: Application
Determining properties like the focal length or refractive index requires optical measurements because the lens maker's formula requires both the radius of curvature and the refractive index. A spherometer measures purely mechanical and geometric dimensions.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Thus, with the help of a spherometer, we can directly measure the radius of curvature of the curved surface.

answer.text: radius of curvature of the curved surface.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q08 - Glow of bulb connected with inductor coil

questiontext.text: A light bulb and an inductor coil are connected to an ac source through a key as shown in the figure below. The key is closed and after sometime an iron rod is inserted into the interior of the inductor. The glow of the light bulb

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
An inductor coil and a light bulb (acting as a resistor \(R\)) are connected in series across an alternating current (AC) source. An iron rod is inserted into the core of the inductor coil.

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
• Self-inductance of an inductor coil: \(L \propto \mu_r\), where \(\mu_r\) is the relative magnetic permeability of the core material.
• Inductive reactance: \(X_L = \omega L\)
• Total circuit impedance: \(Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2}\)
• Root-mean-square circuit current: \(I_{\text{rms}} = \frac{V_{\text{rms}}}{Z}\)
• Power dissipated in the bulb: \(P = I_{\text{rms}}^2 R\)

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
1. Iron is a ferromagnetic material having a very large relative permeability (\(\mu_r \gg 1\)). When the iron rod is inserted into the inductor, the magnetic permeability inside the coil increases substantially, causing its self-inductance \(L\) to increase.
2. With higher inductance \(L\), the inductive reactance \(X_L = \omega L\) increases.
3. An increase in \(X_L\) increases the total impedance \(Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2}\) of the series RL circuit.
4. For a constant source voltage \(V_{\text{rms}}\), the increased impedance causes the current \(I_{\text{rms}}\) flowing through the circuit to decrease.
5. Since the glow of the bulb is governed by the power consumed (\(P = I_{\text{rms}}^2 R\)), a reduction in current results in decreased brightness.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The glow of the light bulb decreases.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q09 - Efficiency dependence of an ideal Carnot engine

questiontext.text: The efficiency of a Carnot engine depends upon

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A Carnot engine is an ideal reversible heat engine operating between two thermal reservoirs: a heat source at absolute temperature \(T_{\text{source}}\) and a heat sink at absolute temperature \(T_{\text{sink}}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
The thermal efficiency \(\eta\) of a Carnot cycle is given by:
\[\eta = 1 - \frac{T_{\text{sink}}}{T_{\text{source}}}\]
This expression demonstrates that the efficiency is strictly a function of the absolute temperatures of the heat source and the heat sink. It does not depend on the working substance, the design of the engine, or the volume of the cylinder.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The efficiency of a Carnot engine depends upon the temperatures of the source and sink.

answer.text: the temperatures of the source and sink.
the volume of the cylinder of the engine.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_SEMICONDUCTORS_MCQ_Q10 - Forward biased diode condition

questiontext.text: Out of the following which one is a forward biased diode?

generalfeedback.text:
Conceptual Principle
A p-n junction diode is forward biased when the potential applied to its anode (p-side), \(V_p\), is strictly greater than the potential applied to its cathode (n-side), \(V_n\): \[V_p > V_n\] If the anode potential is lower than the cathode potential (\(V_p < V_n\)), the diode is reverse biased.

Evaluation of Given Configurations
Evaluating each case with the p-side on the left and the n-side on the right:

  • For \(-4\text{ V}\) at the p-side and \(-2\text{ V}\) at the n-side: \(V_p - V_n = -4\text{ V} - (-2\text{ V}) = -2\text{ V} < 0\), so the diode is reverse biased.
  • For \(2\text{ V}\) at the p-side and \(5\text{ V}\) at the n-side: \(V_p - V_n = 2\text{ V} - 5\text{ V} = -3\text{ V} < 0\), so the diode is reverse biased.
  • For \(-2\text{ V}\) at the p-side and \(+2\text{ V}\) at the n-side: \(V_p - V_n = -2\text{ V} - 2\text{ V} = -4\text{ V} < 0\), so the diode is reverse biased.
  • For \(0\text{ V}\) at the p-side and \(-3\text{ V}\) at the n-side: \(V_p - V_n = 0\text{ V} - (-3\text{ V}) = +3\text{ V} > 0\). Since the p-side is at a higher potential than the n-side, the diode is forward biased.

Final Answer
\(0\text{ V} \quad \text{---}\blacktriangleright|\text{---} \quad -3\text{ V}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q11 - Electric current in single loop circuit

questiontext.text: For the circuit shown in the figure, the current \(I\) will be

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The single closed loop consists of:
• Two DC voltage sources: \(2\text{ V}\) and \(4\text{ V}\), both oriented to drive current in the clockwise direction.
• Three resistors connected in series: \(1\,\Omega\), \(1\,\Omega\), and \(4\,\Omega\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Current \(I\) flows clockwise through all series-connected components. The net electromotive force is the algebraic sum of the source emfs aiding the current.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By Kirchhoff's voltage law or Ohm's law for a closed loop:
\[I = \frac{\sum E}{\sum R}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Calculate the total electromotive force in the loop:
\[E_{\text{net}} = 2\text{ V} + 4\text{ V} = 6\text{ V}\]
2. Calculate the total series resistance:
\[R_{\text{total}} = 1\,\Omega + 1\,\Omega + 4\,\Omega = 6\,\Omega\]
3. Determine the current \(I\):
\[I = \frac{6\text{ V}}{6\,\Omega} = 1\text{ A}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The net driving voltage of \(6\text{ V}\) across a total resistance of \(6\,\Omega\) yields a steady current of \(1\text{ A}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q12 - Phase difference at central interference maximum

questiontext.text: Two coherent sources of light interfere and produce fringe pattern on a screen. For central maximum, the phase difference between the two waves will be

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In an interference pattern produced by two coherent sources, the central maximum is formed at the midpoint of the screen where the paths traversed by the light waves from both sources are identical.

Step 2: Evaluation
The path difference \(\Delta x\) between the two interfering waves at the central fringe is zero:
\[\Delta x = 0\]
The relationship between phase difference \(\Delta \phi\) and path difference \(\Delta x\) is:
\[\Delta \phi = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x\]
Substituting \(\Delta x = 0\) gives:
\[\Delta \phi = 0\]

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The phase difference between the two interfering waves at the central maximum is zero.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q13 - Total energy of hydrogen electron stationary orbit

questiontext.text: The total energy of an electron in the \(n^{\text{th}}\) stationary orbit of the hydrogen atom can be obtained by

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom, the total mechanical energy of an electron in a stationary orbit is negative, signifying that the electron is electrostatically bound to the nucleus.

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The total energy \(E_n\) is related to the principal quantum number \(n\) by:
\[E_n = -\frac{m e^4}{8 \varepsilon_0^2 h^2 n^2}\]
Evaluating the physical constants gives the ground-state energy (\(n = 1\)) as \(-13.6\text{ eV}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substituting this value for any principal quantum number \(n\):
\[E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2}\text{ eV}\]

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The total energy in the \(n^{\text{th}}\) stationary orbit is \(E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2}\text{ eV}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q14 - Mathematical function representing a periodic motion

questiontext.text: Identify the function which represents a periodic motion

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A motion is defined as periodic if it repeats its position and velocity after a fixed interval of time \(T\), satisfying \(f(t + T) = f(t)\).

Step 2: Evaluation
• The exponential functions \(e^{\omega t}\) and \(e^{-\omega t}\) are strictly monotonic functions that grow or decay continuously without repeating.
• The logarithmic function \(\log_2(\omega t)\) is a monotonically increasing function and never repeats its value.
• The function \(\sin \omega t + \cos \omega t\) can be rewritten as:
\[\sin \omega t + \cos \omega t = \sqrt{2}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sin \omega t + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\cos \omega t\right) = \sqrt{2}\sin\left(\omega t + \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\]
Since this is a single sinusoidal function with time period \(T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega}\), it repeats indefinitely with period \(T\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The function representing periodic motion is \(\sin \omega t + \cos \omega t\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q15 - De Broglie wavelength of an electron

questiontext.text: The de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving with kinetic energy of \(144\mathrm{eV}\) is nearly

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Kinetic energy of the electron: \(K = 144\text{ eV}\)
Accelerating potential equivalent: \(V = 144\text{ V}\)

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The de Broglie wavelength \(\lambda\) of an electron accelerated through a potential difference \(V\) is given by:
\[\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2 m_e K}} \approx \frac{1.227}{\sqrt{V}}\text{ nm}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute \(V = 144\text{ V}\):
\[\lambda = \frac{1.227}{\sqrt{144}}\text{ nm} = \frac{1.227}{12}\text{ nm} \approx 0.10225\text{ nm}\]
Expressing in scientific notation with factor \(10^{-3}\):
\[\lambda \approx 102 \times 10^{-3}\text{ nm}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The value \(0.102\text{ nm} = 102 \times 10^{-3}\text{ nm}\) is consistent with the de Broglie wavelength of a non-relativistic electron at \(144\text{ eV}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q16 - Mean free path dependence on molecular diameter

questiontext.text: The mean free path \(l\) for a gas molecule depends upon diameter, \(d\) of the molecule as

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The mean free path \(l\) is the average distance traversed by a gas molecule between successive collisions with other gas molecules.

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
According to the kinetic theory of gases, the mean free path is given by:
\[l = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2} n \pi d^2}\]
where \(n\) is the number density of gas molecules and \(d\) is the effective molecular diameter.

Step 3: Evaluation
For a given number density \(n\), the collision cross-sectional area is \(\pi d^2\). Therefore, the mean free path varies inversely with the square of the molecular diameter:
\[l \propto \frac{1}{d^2}\]

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The mean free path is proportional to \(\frac{1}{d^2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q17 - Collector current in common emitter transistor

questiontext.text: A n-p-n transistor is connected in common emitter configuration (see figure) in which collector voltage drop across load resistance (\(800\,\Omega\)) connected to the collector circuit is \(0.8\mathrm{V}\). The collector current is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Load resistance in collector circuit: \(R_C = 800\,\Omega\)
Voltage drop across the load resistance: \(V_{R_C} = 0.8\text{ V}\)

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By Ohm's law, the current \(I_C\) flowing through the collector load resistance is:
\[I_C = \frac{V_{R_C}}{R_C}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given values:
\[I_C = \frac{0.8\text{ V}}{800\,\Omega} = \frac{8}{8000}\text{ A} = 10^{-3}\text{ A} = 1\text{ mA}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The collector current is \(1\text{ mA}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q18 - Velocity of ball passing a window

questiontext.text:
A person sitting in the ground floor of a building notices through the window, of height \(1.5\mathrm{m}\), a ball dropped from the roof of the building crosses the window in \(0.1\mathrm{s}\). What is the velocity of the ball when it is at the topmost point of the window?

\((g = 10\mathrm{m / s^2})\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Height of the window: \(h = 1.5\text{ m}\)
Time taken to traverse the window: \(t = 0.1\text{ s}\)
Acceleration due to gravity: \(g = 10\text{ m/s}^2\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Take the downward direction as positive. Let \(u\) be the downward velocity of the ball when it reaches the topmost edge of the window.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Using the second equation of motion for constant downward acceleration:
\[h = u t + \frac{1}{2} g t^2\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given values into the kinematic equation:
\[1.5 = u(0.1) + \frac{1}{2}(10)(0.1)^2\]
\[1.5 = 0.1u + 5(0.01)\]
\[1.5 = 0.1u + 0.05\]
Rearranging to solve for \(u\):
\[0.1u = 1.5 - 0.05 = 1.45\]
\[u = \frac{1.45}{0.1} = 14.5\text{ m/s}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The average speed across the window is \(\frac{1.5\text{ m}}{0.1\text{ s}} = 15\text{ m/s}\). Since the average speed in uniformly accelerated motion equals \(u + \frac{1}{2}gt = u + 0.5\text{ m/s}\), setting \(u + 0.5 = 15\) confirms \(u = 14.5\text{ m/s}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q19 - Wavelength calculation from plane electromagnetic wave

questiontext.text:
The magnetic field in a plane electromagnetic wave is given by:

\[B_y = 2 \times 10^{-7} \sin (\pi \times 10^3 x + 3\pi \times 10^{11} t)\text{ T}\]

Calculate the wavelength.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The wave equation for the magnetic field component is:
\[B_y = 2 \times 10^{-7} \sin (\pi \times 10^3 x + 3\pi \times 10^{11} t)\text{ T}\]

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Comparing the given field with the standard harmonic wave equation:
\[B = B_0 \sin(k x + \omega t)\]
where \(k\) is the propagation constant (angular wave number). The wavelength \(\lambda\) is related to \(k\) by:
\[\lambda = \frac{2\pi}{k}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
From the equation, the wave number is:
\[k = \pi \times 10^3\text{ m}^{-1}\]
Compute the wavelength \(\lambda\):
\[\lambda = \frac{2\pi}{\pi \times 10^3} = \frac{2}{10^3} = 2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The wave speed is \(v = \frac{\omega}{k} = \frac{3\pi \times 10^{11}}{\pi \times 10^3} = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\), which equals the speed of light in vacuum. The wavelength is \(2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q20 - Position of pressing string for desired frequency

questiontext.text: The length of the string of a musical instrument is \(90~\mathrm{cm}\) and has a fundamental frequency of \(120\mathrm{Hz}\). Where should it be pressed to produce fundamental frequency of \(180\mathrm{Hz}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial vibrating length of the string: \(L_1 = 90\text{ cm}\)
Initial fundamental frequency: \(f_1 = 120\text{ Hz}\)
Desired fundamental frequency: \(f_2 = 180\text{ Hz}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The tension \(T\) in the string and its linear mass density \(\mu\) remain unchanged when pressing the string against a fret.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The fundamental frequency of a vibrating stretched string fixed at both ends is given by:
\[f = \frac{v}{2L} = \frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}\]
Therefore, frequency is inversely proportional to the vibrating length:
\[f \propto \frac{1}{L} \implies f_1 L_1 = f_2 L_2\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given values into the inverse proportionality relation:
\[120 \times 90 = 180 \times L_2\]
Solve for the new vibrating length \(L_2\):
\[L_2 = \frac{120 \times 90}{180} = \frac{120}{2} = 60\text{ cm}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since frequency increases from \(120\text{ Hz}\) to \(180\text{ Hz}\) by a factor of \(1.5\), the length must decrease by a factor of \(1.5\): \(\frac{90\text{ cm}}{1.5} = 60\text{ cm}\). The string should be pressed to provide an effective length of \(60\text{ cm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q21 - Acceleration of electron due to proton attraction

questiontext.text: The acceleration of an electron due to the mutual attraction between the electron and a proton when they are \(1.6\text{ \AA}\) apart is, \((m_e \approx 9\times 10^{-31}\mathrm{kg}, e = 1.6\times 10^{-19}\mathrm{C})\) \(\left(\text{Take } \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \mathrm{N m}^2 \mathrm{C}^{-2}\right)\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Distance between electron and proton: \(r = 1.6\text{ \AA} = 1.6 \times 10^{-10}\text{ m}\)
Elementary charge: \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\)
Mass of electron: \(m_e = 9 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}\)
Coulomb constant: \(\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^2\text{C}^{-2}\)

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The electrostatic attractive force between the charges is given by Coulomb's law:
\[F = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{e^2}{r^2}\]
The resulting acceleration of the electron is given by Newton's second law:
\[a = \frac{F}{m_e}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
1. Calculate the electrostatic force:
\[F = \frac{(9 \times 10^9) \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{(1.6 \times 10^{-10})^2}\]
\[F = \frac{9 \times 10^9 \times 2.56 \times 10^{-38}}{2.56 \times 10^{-20}} = 9 \times 10^9 \times 10^{-18} = 9 \times 10^{-9}\text{ N}\]
2. Calculate the acceleration of the electron:
\[a = \frac{9 \times 10^{-9}\text{ N}}{9 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}} = 10^{22}\text{ m/s}^2\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The calculated acceleration is \(10^{22}\text{ m/s}^2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q22 - Experimental verification of wave nature of electrons

questiontext.text: The wave nature of electrons was experimentally verified by,

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
While Louis de Broglie hypothesized the wave-particle duality of matter in 1924 by proposing matter waves with wavelength \(\lambda = \frac{h}{p}\), this hypothesis required experimental confirmation.

Step 2: Evaluation
In 1927, C.J. Davisson and L.H. Germer performed an experiment observing the diffraction of an electron beam scattered by a nickel crystal. The observed diffraction peaks quantitatively confirmed Bragg's diffraction condition for the de Broglie wavelength of electrons.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The wave nature of electrons was experimentally verified by Davisson and Germer.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q23 - Ratio of cross sectional areas of conductors

questiontext.text: Two solid conductors are made up of same material, have same length and same resistance. One of them has a circular cross section of area \(\mathrm{A}_1\) and the other one has a square cross section of area \(\mathrm{A}_2\). The ratio \(\frac{\mathrm{A}_1}{\mathrm{A}_2}\) is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Two conductors have:
• Same material: \(\rho_1 = \rho_2 = \rho\)
• Same length: \(l_1 = l_2 = l\)
• Same electrical resistance: \(R_1 = R_2 = R\)
Cross-sectional areas: \(A_1\) (circular) and \(A_2\) (square).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The electrical resistance of a uniform conductor is given by:
\[R = \rho \frac{l}{A}\]
Solving for area of cross section:
\[A = \frac{\rho l}{R}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Since the resistivity \(\rho\), length \(l\), and resistance \(R\) are identical for both conductors:
\[A_1 = \frac{\rho l}{R} \quad \text{and} \quad A_2 = \frac{\rho l}{R}\]
Taking the ratio of the cross-sectional areas:
\[\frac{A_1}{A_2} = \frac{\frac{\rho l}{R}}{\frac{\rho l}{R}} = 1\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The geometrical shape of the cross section does not alter the required area when length, material resistivity, and resistance are all identical. The ratio \(\frac{A_1}{A_2}\) is \(1\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q24 - Kirchhoff loop rule for closed mesh

questiontext.text: For the circuit given below, the Kirchoff's loop rule for the loop BCDEB is given by the equation

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Loop BCDEB elements:
• Branch BC: resistor \(R_2\) carrying current \(i_2\) directed from B to C.
• Branch CD: source of emf \(E_2\), with its positive plate at C and negative plate at D.
• Branch DE: source of emf \(E_3\), with its negative plate at D and positive plate at E.
• Branch EB: resistor \(R_1\) carrying current \(i_3\) directed downward from B to E.

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
According to Kirchhoff's loop rule (KVL), the algebraic sum of the changes in potential across all elements encountered in traversing a closed loop is zero:
\[\sum \Delta V = 0\]
Sign convention:
• Traversing along the direction of current across a resistor gives a potential drop: \(-iR\).
• Traversing against the direction of current across a resistor gives a potential rise: \(+iR\).
• Traversing a cell from positive to negative terminal gives a potential drop: \(-E\).
• Traversing a cell from negative to positive terminal gives a potential rise: \(+E\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Traverse loop BCDEB starting at node B and returning to B:
1. From B to C (along current \(i_2\)): \(-i_2 R_2\)
2. From C to D (from positive to negative terminal of \(E_2\)): \(-E_2\)
3. From D to E (from negative to positive terminal of \(E_3\)): \(+E_3\)
4. From E to B (against current \(i_3\)): \(+i_3 R_1\)
Summing the potential differences around the loop:
\[-i_2 R_2 - E_2 + E_3 + i_3 R_1 = 0\]
Multiplying the entire equation by \(-1\):
\[i_2 R_2 - E_2 + E_3 - i_3 R_1 = 0\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Both forms represent the identical physical constraint, and the resulting relation is \(i_2 R_2 - E_2 + E_3 - i_3 R_1 = 0\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q25 - Star surface temperatures and blackbody radiation

questiontext.text: Three stars A, B, C have surface temperatures \(\mathrm{T_A}\), \(\mathrm{T_B}\), \(\mathrm{T_C}\) respectively. Star A appears bluish, star B appears reddish and star C yellowish. Hence,

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to Wien's displacement law, the wavelength \(\lambda_{\text{max}}\) corresponding to maximum emission intensity of a blackbody is inversely proportional to its absolute temperature \(T\):
\[\lambda_{\text{max}} T = b \implies T \propto \frac{1}{\lambda_{\text{max}}}\]

Step 2: Evaluation
In the visible spectrum, the wavelengths of the perceived colours are ordered as:
\[\lambda_{\text{blue}} < \lambda_{\text{yellow}} < \lambda_{\text{red}}\]
Since temperature is inversely related to dominant peak wavelength:
\[T_{\text{blue}} > T_{\text{yellow}} > T_{\text{red}}\]

Step 3: Application
• Star A is bluish \(\implies T_{\text{A}} = T_{\text{blue}}\)
• Star C is yellowish \(\implies T_{\text{C}} = T_{\text{yellow}}\)
• Star B is reddish \(\implies T_{\text{B}} = T_{\text{red}}\)
Arranging their temperatures in descending order:
\[\mathrm{T_A} > \mathrm{T_C} > \mathrm{T_B}\]

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct relationship among the surface temperatures is \(\mathrm{T_A > T_C > T_B}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q26 - Angle of contact and surface wetting

questiontext.text: A liquid does not wet the solid surface if angle of contact is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The angle of contact \(\theta\) between a liquid and a solid depends on the relative magnitudes of adhesive forces (between liquid and solid molecules) and cohesive forces (between liquid molecules themselves).

Step 2: Evaluation
• When adhesive forces dominate over cohesive forces, the liquid spreads across the solid, forming an acute angle of contact (\(\theta < 90^\circ\)), and the liquid wets the surface.
• When cohesive forces dominate over adhesive forces, the liquid minimizes its contact area with the solid, forming an obtuse angle of contact (\(\theta > 90^\circ\)), and the liquid does not wet the solid surface (as seen with mercury on glass).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A liquid does not wet a solid surface if the angle of contact is greater than \(90^\circ\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q27 - String tension at vertical circle bottom

questiontext.text: A point mass \(m\) is moved in a vertical circle of radius \(r\) with the help of a string. The velocity of the mass is \(\sqrt{7gr}\) at the lowest point. The tension in the string at the lowest point is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of the particle: \(m\)
Radius of the vertical circular path: \(r\)
Speed at the lowest point: \(v = \sqrt{7gr}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
At the lowest point, the tension \(T\) acts vertically upward toward the centre of the circle, while gravity \(mg\) acts vertically downward.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The net upward radial force provides the required centripetal acceleration:
\[T - mg = \frac{m v^2}{r}\]
Solving for the tension \(T\):
\[T = mg + \frac{m v^2}{r}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute \(v^2 = (\sqrt{7gr})^2 = 7gr\):
\[T = mg + \frac{m(7gr)}{r} = mg + 7mg = 8mg\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The tension at the lowest point must balance the weight of the particle and provide the centripetal force. The total tension is \(8mg\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q28 - Image distance in a concave mirror

questiontext.text: An object is placed on the principal axis of a concave mirror at a distance of \(1.5f\) (\(f\) is the focal length). The image will be at,

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Concave mirror focal length magnitude: \(f\)
Object distance magnitude: \(1.5f\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Using Cartesian sign conventions with pole as the origin:
• Focal length: \(f_{\text{mirror}} = -f\)
• Object distance: \(u = -1.5f\)

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The mirror formula relating object distance \(u\), image distance \(v\), and focal length is:
\[\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f_{\text{mirror}}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute \(u = -1.5f = -\frac{3}{2}f\) and \(f_{\text{mirror}} = -f\):
\[\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{-\frac{3}{2}f} = \frac{1}{-f}\]
\[\frac{1}{v} - \frac{2}{3f} = -\frac{1}{f}\]
Solve for \(\frac{1}{v}\):
\[\frac{1}{v} = -\frac{1}{f} + \frac{2}{3f} = -\frac{3}{3f} + \frac{2}{3f} = -\frac{1}{3f}\]
Taking the reciprocal gives:
\[v = -3f\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since the object lies between the centre of curvature (\(2f\)) and focus (\(f\)), a real, inverted, magnified image forms beyond the centre of curvature on the same side as the object (\(v = -3f\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q29 - Activity of a radioactive alpha decay sample

questiontext.text: The half life of radioactive sample undergoing \(\alpha\) decay is \(1.4 \times 10^{17}\text{ s}\). If the number of nuclei in the sample is \(2.0 \times 10^{21}\), the activity of the sample is nearly

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Half-life of the radioactive isotope: \(T_{1/2} = 1.4 \times 10^{17}\text{ s}\)
Number of undecayed radioactive nuclei: \(N = 2.0 \times 10^{21}\)

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The decay constant \(\lambda\) is related to half-life by:
\[\lambda = \frac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}} \approx \frac{0.693}{T_{1/2}}\]
The activity \(A\) of the sample is defined as the rate of decay:
\[A = \lambda N = \frac{0.693 \times N}{T_{1/2}}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given values into the activity formula:
\[A = \frac{0.693 \times 2.0 \times 10^{21}}{1.4 \times 10^{17}\text{ s}}\]
\[A = \frac{1.386 \times 10^{21}}{1.4 \times 10^{17}} = 0.99 \times 10^4\text{ Bq} \approx 10^4\text{ Bq}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The activity is approximately \(10^4\text{ Bq}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q30 - Velocity of light from critical angle

questiontext.text: If the critical angle for total internal reflection from a medium to vacuum is \(45^{\circ}\), then velocity of light in the medium is,

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Critical angle for total internal reflection: \(C = 45^{\circ}\)
Speed of light in vacuum: \(c = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\)

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The refractive index \(\mu\) of the medium with respect to vacuum is related to the critical angle \(C\) by Snell's law at the critical condition:
\[\mu = \frac{1}{\sin C}\]
The velocity of light \(v\) in a medium with refractive index \(\mu\) is given by:
\[v = \frac{c}{\mu} = c \sin C\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute \(C = 45^{\circ}\) and \(c = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\):
\[\sin 45^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\]
\[v = (3 \times 10^8) \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Since \(\mu = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414 > 1\), the velocity in the medium is less than \(c\). The velocity of light in the medium is \(\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q31 - Induced emf in rotating metallic wheel

questiontext.text: A wheel with \(20\) metallic spokes each \(1\mathrm{~m}\) long is rotated with a speed of \(120\mathrm{~rpm}\) in a plane perpendicular to a magnetic field of \(0.4\mathrm{~G}\). The induced emf between the axle and rim of the wheel will be, \((1\mathrm{~G} = 10^{-4}\mathrm{~T})\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Number of metallic spokes: \(N = 20\)
Length of each spoke (radius of wheel): \(l = 1\text{ m}\)
Rotational speed: \(n = 120\text{ rpm}\)
Magnetic field: \(B = 0.4\text{ G} = 0.4 \times 10^{-4}\text{ T}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The spokes rotate in a plane perpendicular to the uniform magnetic field. Since all spokes are identical and connected in parallel between the common axle and outer rim, the net induced electromotive force equals the emf developed across a single spoke.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The angular velocity is:
\[\omega = \frac{2\pi n}{60}\]
The motional emf induced across a rod of length \(l\) rotating about one end in a perpendicular magnetic field is:
\[e = \frac{1}{2} B \omega l^2\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Calculate angular speed \(\omega\):
\[\omega = \frac{2\pi \times 120}{60} = 4\pi\text{ rad/s}\]
2. Substitute \(B\), \(\omega\), and \(l\):
\[e = \frac{1}{2} \times (0.4 \times 10^{-4}\text{ T}) \times (4\pi\text{ rad/s}) \times (1\text{ m})^2\]
\[e = 0.8\pi \times 10^{-4}\text{ V} \approx 0.8 \times 3.1416 \times 10^{-4}\text{ V} \approx 2.513 \times 10^{-4}\text{ V}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The induced emf between the axle and rim is \(2.51 \times 10^{-4}\text{ V}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q32 - Physical meaning of variables in gas law

questiontext.text: An ideal gas equation can be written as \(P = \frac{\rho R T}{M_0}\) where \(\rho\) and \(M_0\) are respectively,

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The ideal gas equation in terms of total mass \(m\) and molar mass \(M_0\) is given by:
\[P V = n R T = \left(\frac{m}{M_0}\right) R T\]

Step 2: Evaluation
Rearranging the expression by dividing both sides by volume \(V\):
\[P = \left(\frac{m}{V}\right)\frac{R T}{M_0}\]
Here, the ratio \(\frac{m}{V}\) represents the mass density \(\rho\) of the gas, while \(M_0\) represents the molar mass of the gas.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
In the equation \(P = \frac{\rho R T}{M_0}\), \(\rho\) is the mass density and \(M_0\) is the molar mass.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q33 - Potential variation with distance from charged shell

questiontext.text: The variation of electrostatic potential with radial distance \(r\) from the centre of a positively charged metallic thin shell of radius \(R\) is given by the graph

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For a thin conducting spherical shell carrying total charge \(Q\), the electric field inside the shell is zero (\(E = 0\) for \(r < R\)) due to electrostatic shielding. Outside the shell (\(r \ge R\)), the electric field behaves as if all the charge were concentrated at the centre.

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Electric field is related to potential gradient by \(E = -\frac{dV}{dr}\).
• Inside and on the surface of the shell (\(r \le R\)):
\[E = 0 \implies V(r) = \text{constant} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q}{R}\]
• Outside the shell (\(r > R\)):
\[V(r) = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q}{r} \propto \frac{1}{r}\]

Step 3: Evaluation
The electrostatic potential \(V\) remains constant from \(r = 0\) to \(r = R\) at a finite positive value, and for \(r > R\), it decreases hyperbolically as \(\frac{1}{r}\) toward zero.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct profile is a flat horizontal line from \(r = 0\) to \(r = R\), followed by a continuous curve dropping inversely with \(r\).

Step 2: Evaluation

• The NAND gate and the NOR gate are universal gates because repeated suitable combinations of either can synthesize all other logic operations.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q35 - Thermodynamic process identification from PV diagram

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q36 - Refractive index of a biconvex lens

questiontext.text: The power of a biconvex lens is \(10\text{ dioptre}\) and the radius of curvature of each surface is \(10\mathrm{~cm}\). Then the refractive index of the material of the lens is,

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Optical power of the lens: \(P = 10\text{ D}\)
Radii of curvature of surfaces: \(R_1 = +10\text{ cm}\) and \(R_2 = -10\text{ cm}\)

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The focal length \(f\) is given by:
\[f = \frac{1}{P}\]
The lens maker's formula is:
\[\frac{1}{f} = (\mu - 1)\left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right)\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
1. Calculate the focal length in centimetres:
\[f = \frac{1}{10}\text{ m} = 0.1\text{ m} = 10\text{ cm}\]
2. Substitute \(f = 10\text{ cm}\), \(R_1 = 10\text{ cm}\), and \(R_2 = -10\text{ cm}\):
\[\frac{1}{10} = (\mu - 1)\left(\frac{1}{10} - \left(-\frac{1}{10}\right)\right)\]
\[\frac{1}{10} = (\mu - 1)\left(\frac{2}{10}\right)\]
3. Solve for \(\mu\):
\[1 = 2(\mu - 1) \implies \mu - 1 = \frac{1}{2} \implies \mu = 1 + \frac{1}{2} = \frac{3}{2}\]

The calculated refractive index of the material is \(\frac{3}{2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q37 - Dopant for n-type extrinsic semiconductor

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q38 - Liquid column height in custom barometer

questiontext.text: A barometer is constructed using a liquid (density = \(760\mathrm{~kg/m^3}\)). What would be the height of the liquid column, when a mercury barometer reads \(76\mathrm{~cm}\)? (density of mercury = \(13600\mathrm{~kg/m^3}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Density of custom liquid: \(\rho_1 = 760\text{ kg/m}^3\)
Height of mercury column: \(h_2 = 76\text{ cm} = 0.76\text{ m}\)
Density of mercury: \(\rho_2 = 13600\text{ kg/m}^3\)

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The atmospheric pressure supported by both barometer columns must be identical:
\[P_{\text{atm}} = \rho_1 g h_1 = \rho_2 g h_2\]
Equating pressures yields:
\[h_1 = \frac{\rho_2 h_2}{\rho_1}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the numerical values:
\[h_1 = \frac{13600\text{ kg/m}^3 \times 0.76\text{ m}}{760\text{ kg/m}^3}\]

Because the density of the liquid is \(\frac{13600}{760} \approx 17.89\) times smaller than that of mercury, the column must be proportionally taller. The required height is \(13.6\text{ m}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q39 - Magnetic moment of circular current loop

questiontext.text: A wire of length \(L\text{ metre}\) carrying a current of \(I\text{ ampere}\) is bent in the form of a circle. Its magnetic moment is,

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Total length of wire: \(L\)
Current carried by wire: \(I\)
Shape formed: single circular loop of radius \(R\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The circumference of the circle equals the wire length:
\[L = 2\pi R \implies R = \frac{L}{2\pi}\]
The enclosed cross-sectional area of the loop is:
\[A = \pi R^2\]
The magnetic dipole moment \(M\) of a planar current-carrying loop is given by:
\[M = I A\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute \(R = \frac{L}{2\pi}\) into the area equation:
\[A = \pi \left(\frac{L}{2\pi}\right)^2 = \pi \frac{L^2}{4\pi^2} = \frac{L^2}{4\pi}\]
Compute the magnetic moment:
\[M = I \left(\frac{L^2}{4\pi}\right) = \frac{I L^2}{4\pi}\text{ A}\cdot\text{m}^2\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The units are \(\text{A}\cdot\text{m}^2\). The magnetic moment is \(I L^2 / 4\pi\text{ A m}^2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q40 - Capacitance ratio with dielectric slab insertion

questiontext.text: A parallel plate capacitor having cross-sectional area \(A\) and separation \(d\) has air in between the plates. Now an insulating slab of same area but thickness \(d/2\) is inserted between the plates as shown in figure having dielectric constant \(K\) (\(= 4\)). The ratio of new capacitance to its original capacitance will be,

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Original plate separation: \(d\)
Plate area: \(A\)
Thickness of insulating slab: \(t = \frac{d}{2}\)
Dielectric constant: \(K = 4\)

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Original capacitance with air between plates:
\[C_0 = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}\]
Capacitance with a dielectric slab of thickness \(t\) and constant \(K\):
\[C = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d - t + \frac{t}{K}}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute \(t = \frac{d}{2}\) and \(K = 4\):
\[d - t + \frac{t}{K} = d - \frac{d}{2} + \frac{d/2}{4} = \frac{d}{2} + \frac{d}{8} = \frac{5d}{8}\]
Thus, the new capacitance is:
\[C = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{\frac{5d}{8}} = \frac{8}{5} \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d} = \frac{8}{5} C_0\]
Take the ratio of new to original capacitance:
\[\frac{C}{C_0} = \frac{8}{5} = 8 : 5\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The ratio of the new capacitance to its original capacitance is \(8 : 5\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q41 - Depth for fractional acceleration due gravity

questiontext.text: What is the depth at which the value of acceleration due to gravity becomes \(1/n\) times the value that at the surface of earth? (radius of earth \(= R\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Acceleration due to gravity at depth \(d\): \(g' = \frac{g}{n}\)
Radius of the earth: \(R\)

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The variation of acceleration due to gravity with depth \(d\) below the surface of the earth is given by:
\[g' = g\left(1 - \frac{d}{R}\right)\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Equating \(g'\) to \(\frac{g}{n}\):
\[\frac{g}{n} = g\left(1 - \frac{d}{R}\right)\]
Divide both sides by \(g\):
\[\frac{1}{n} = 1 - \frac{d}{R}\]
Rearrange to isolate the ratio \(\frac{d}{R}\):
\[\frac{d}{R} = 1 - \frac{1}{n} = \frac{n - 1}{n}\]
Solve for the depth \(d\):
\[d = \frac{R(n - 1)}{n}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
For \(n = 1\), \(d = 0\) (at surface), and as \(n \to \infty\), \(d \to R\) (at centre of Earth where \(g = 0\)). The required depth is \(R(n - 1)/n\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q42 - Percentage relative error of time measurements

questiontext.text:
Time intervals measured by a clock give the following readings:

\(1.25\mathrm{~s}, 1.24\mathrm{~s}, 1.27\mathrm{~s}, 1.21\mathrm{~s}\) and \(1.28\mathrm{~s}\).

What is the percentage relative error of the observations?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Measured time observations: \(T_1 = 1.25\text{ s}\), \(T_2 = 1.24\text{ s}\), \(T_3 = 1.27\text{ s}\), \(T_4 = 1.21\text{ s}\), and \(T_5 = 1.28\text{ s}\).
Total number of readings: \(N = 5\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
• Mean value: \(T_{\text{mean}} = \frac{\sum T_i}{N}\)
• Absolute errors: \(\Delta T_i = |T_i - T_{\text{mean}}|\)
• Mean absolute error: \(\overline{\Delta T} = \frac{\sum \Delta T_i}{N}\)
• Percentage relative error: \(\text{Percentage Error} = \frac{\overline{\Delta T}}{T_{\text{mean}}} \times 100\%\)

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
1. Calculate the mean time:
\[T_{\text{mean}} = \frac{1.25 + 1.24 + 1.27 + 1.21 + 1.28}{5} = \frac{6.25}{5} = 1.25\text{ s}\]
2. Calculate the individual absolute errors:
\[|\Delta T_1| = |1.25 - 1.25| = 0.00\text{ s}\]
\[|\Delta T_2| = |1.24 - 1.25| = 0.01\text{ s}\]
\[|\Delta T_3| = |1.27 - 1.25| = 0.02\text{ s}\]

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q43 - Position vector of centre of mass

questiontext.text: Three identical spheres, each of mass \(M\), are placed at the corners of a right angle triangle with mutually perpendicular sides equal to \(2\mathrm{~m}\) (see figure). Taking the point of intersection of the two mutually perpendicular sides as the origin, find the position vector of centre of mass.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Three identical particles of mass \(M\) each:
• Sphere 1 at origin \((0, 0)\): \(\vec{r}_1 = 0\hat{i} + 0\hat{j}\)
• Sphere 2 on the \(x\)-axis at \((2\text{ m}, 0)\): \(\vec{r}_2 = 2\hat{i}\)
• Sphere 3 on the \(y\)-axis at \((0, 2\text{ m})\): \(\vec{r}_3 = 2\hat{j}\)
Total mass of system: \(M_{\text{total}} = 3M\)

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The position vector of the centre of mass of a discrete system of particles is given by:
\[\vec{r}_{\text{CM}} = \frac{\sum m_i \vec{r}_i}{\sum m_i}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the respective masses and coordinates:
\[\vec{r}_{\text{CM}} = \frac{M(0) + M(2\hat{i}) + M(2\hat{j})}{M + M + M}\]
\[\vec{r}_{\text{CM}} = \frac{2M(\hat{i} + \hat{j})}{3M} = \frac{2}{3}(\hat{i} + \hat{j})\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
By symmetry, the centre of mass lies along the line \(y = x\) at \(x_{\text{CM}} = y_{\text{CM}} = \frac{0 + 2 + 0}{3} = \frac{2}{3}\text{ m}\). The position vector is \(\frac{2}{3}(\hat{i} + \hat{j})\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_2020_MCQ_Q44 - Equivalent resistance of symmetric bridge network

questiontext.text: The equivalent resistance between A and B for the mesh shown in the figure is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The resistor network consists of:
• A top triangular section with upper branches containing a \(4\,\Omega\) resistor and an \(8\,\Omega\) resistor in series, bridged across a horizontal resistor of \(6\,\Omega\).
• Two lower branches leading to terminals A and B with resistors of \(4\,\Omega\) and \(8\,\Omega\) respectively.

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
• Series resistance: \(R_{\text{series}} = R_1 + R_2\)
• Parallel resistance: \(\frac{1}{R_p} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} \implies R_p = \frac{R_1 R_2}{R_1 + R_2}\)

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
1. Evaluate the top apex combination:
The upper \(4\,\Omega\) and \(8\,\Omega\) resistors are in series:
\[R_{\text{top}} = 4\,\Omega + 8\,\Omega = 12\,\Omega\]
2. This \(12\,\Omega\) branch is connected in parallel with the central horizontal \(6\,\Omega\) resistor:
\[R_{\text{parallel}} = \frac{12 \times 6}{12 + 6} = \frac{72}{18} = 4\,\Omega\]
3. The reduced network now consists of three elements in series between terminal A and terminal B:
• Lower left resistor: \(4\,\Omega\)
• Equivalent middle section: \(4\,\Omega\)
• Lower right resistor: \(8\,\Omega\)
Calculate the total equivalent resistance \(R_{AB}\):
\[R_{AB} = 4\,\Omega + 4\,\Omega + 8\,\Omega = 16\,\Omega\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Summing the series and parallel reductions yields \(16\,\Omega\).

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_PHYSICS_Q45 - Acceleration of block and trolley system

questiontext.text: Calculate the acceleration of the block and trolley system shown in the figure. The co-efficient of kinetic friction between the trolley and the surface is \(0.05\). (\(g = 10\text{ m/s}^2\), mass of the string is negligible and no other friction exists).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of the trolley on the horizontal surface, \(M = 10\text{ kg}\).
Mass of the hanging block, \(m = 2\text{ kg}\).
Coefficient of kinetic friction between the trolley and horizontal surface, \(\mu_k = 0.05\).
Acceleration due to gravity, \(g = 10\text{ m/s}^2\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The string is light and inextensible, so both the trolley and the hanging block move with the same magnitude of acceleration \(a\). Let the downward direction for the hanging block and the forward horizontal direction for the trolley be taken as positive.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Normal reaction on the trolley: \(N = M g\).
Kinetic friction opposing the motion of the trolley: \(f_k = \mu_k N = \mu_k M g\).
Equation of motion for the hanging block of mass \(m\):
\[m g - T = m a\]
Equation of motion for the trolley of mass \(M\):
\[T - f_k = M a\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Adding the two equations of motion gives:
\[m g - f_k = (M + m) a\]
\[a = \frac{m g - \mu_k M g}{M + m}\]
Substitute the given values:
\[m g = 2 \times 10 = 20\text{ N}\]
\[f_k = 0.05 \times 10 \times 10 = 5\text{ N}\]
\[M + m = 10 + 2 = 12\text{ kg}\]
\[a = \frac{20 - 5}{12} = \frac{15}{12} = 1.25\text{ m/s}^2\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The net pulling force is \(15\text{ N}\) acting on a total system mass of \(12\text{ kg}\), giving an acceleration of \(1.25\text{ m/s}^2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_CHEMISTRY_Q46 - Incorrect statement about acid rain

questiontext.text: Which of the following statement is NOT true about acid rain?

Acid rain results from the emission of oxides of sulfur and nitrogen (\(\text{SO}_2\) and \(\text{NO}_2\)) as well as \(\text{CO}_2\), which dissolve in moisture to form sulfurous, sulfuric, nitric, and carbonic acids. Rainwater is considered acidic when its pH falls below \(5.6\).

Step 2: Evaluation of Acid Rain Effects
Acid rain reacts chemically with calcium carbonate present in marble monuments such as the Taj Mahal via the reaction:

This causes discoloration, pitting, and erosion of the stone (marble cancer), causing significant damage to monuments. Acid rain also leaches essential nutrients from soil and damages plant foliage.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_CHEMISTRY_Q47 - Oxidation state of underlined atom

questiontext.text:
The oxidation number of the underlined atom in the following species are given:

(a) Cu\(_2\)O is \(-1\)
(b) ClO\(_3^-\) is \(+5\)
(c) K\(_2\)Cr\(_2\)O\(_7\) is \(+6\)
(d) HAuCl\(_4\) is \(+3\)

Identify the incorrect option.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The sum of oxidation numbers of all atoms in a neutral molecule is zero, and in a polyatomic ion it equals the charge of the ion.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Species
1. In cuprous oxide (\(\text{Cu}_2\text{O}\)): oxygen has an oxidation state of \(-2\). Therefore, \(2x + (-2) = 0 \implies 2x = +2 \implies x = +1\). Thus, copper has an oxidation state of \(+1\), not \(-1\).
2. In chlorate ion (\(\text{ClO}_3^-\)): \(x + 3(-2) = -1 \implies x - 6 = -1 \implies x = +5\). This is correct.
3. In potassium dichromate (\(\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7\)): \(2(+1) + 2x + 7(-2) = 0 \implies 2 + 2x - 14 = 0 \implies 2x = 12 \implies x = +6\). This is correct.
4. In chloroauric acid (\(\text{HAuCl}_4\)): \(+1 + x + 4(-1) = 0 \implies x - 3 = 0 \implies x = +3\). This is correct.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The statement stating that the oxidation state of copper in \(\text{Cu}_2\text{O}\) is \(-1\) is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_CHEMISTRY_Q48 - Hoffmann bromamide degradation of propanamide

questiontext.text: Reaction of propanamide with ethanolic sodium hydroxide and bromine will give

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The reaction of a primary carboxamide with bromine in the presence of an aqueous or ethanolic solution of sodium hydroxide is the Hoffmann bromamide degradation reaction.

Step 2: Reaction Mechanism and Stoichiometry
In this reaction, the carbonyl group of the amide is eliminated as carbonate, and the alkyl group migrates to nitrogen, producing a primary amine containing one fewer carbon atom than the parent amide:
\[\text{R-CONH}_2 + \text{Br}_2 + 4\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{R-NH}_2 + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 + 2\text{NaBr} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\]

Step 3: Application to Propanamide
Propanamide has three carbons: \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2\). Loss of the carbonyl carbon yields ethylamine (\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2\)):
\[\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2 + \text{Br}_2 + 4\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2 + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 + 2\text{NaBr} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\]

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The product obtained is ethylamine.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_CHEMISTRY_Q49 - Conditions for purification by steam distillation

questiontext.text: A liquid compound (x) can be purified by steam distillation only if it is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Steam distillation is a separation technique applied to separate substances that are steam volatile and practically immiscible with water.

Step 2: Evaluation of Conditions
In steam distillation, the mixture boils at a temperature lower than the boiling points of both water and the organic liquid, when the sum of their individual vapor pressures equals atmospheric pressure: \(P = p_{\text{water}} + p_{\text{compound}} = P_{\text{atm}}\). For this to work effectively, the compound must exert sufficient vapor pressure near \(100^\circ\text{C}\) (steam volatile) and must not dissolve significantly in water (immiscible with water), allowing the organic component to separate out easily as a distinct layer upon condensation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The required conditions are that the compound is steam volatile and immiscible with water.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_CHEMISTRY_Q50 - Linear molecular geometry

questiontext.text: Among the compounds shown below which one revealed a linear structure?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Molecular geometry is determined by the arrangement of electron pairs (bonding and non-bonding) around the central atom according to VSEPR theory and hybridization.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Molecule
1. \(\text{NO}_2\): Nitrogen has an odd electron and forms two bonds with oxygen atoms; the molecule is bent (angular) with a bond angle of about \(134^\circ\).
2. \(\text{HOCl}\): The central oxygen atom has two single bonds (to \(\text{H}\) and \(\text{Cl}\)) and two lone pairs, resulting in a bent structure with a bond angle around \(102^\circ\).
3. \(\text{O}_3\): The central oxygen has one single bond, one double bond, and one lone pair (\(sp^2\) hybridization), giving a bent shape with a bond angle of approximately \(117^\circ\).
4. \(\text{N}_2\text{O}\): The central nitrogen atom is \(sp\)-hybridized, bonded to the terminal nitrogen and oxygen without lone pairs on the central atom (resonance structures \(\text{N}\equiv\text{N}^+-\text{O}^- \leftrightarrow \text{N}^-=\text{N}^+=\text{O}\)). This gives a linear geometry with a bond angle of \(180^\circ\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\text{N}_2\text{O}\) exhibits a linear structure.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_CHEMISTRY_Q51 - Most reactive compound in electrophilic aromatic substitution

questiontext.text: Which of the following compound is most reactive in electrophilic aromatic substitution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The rate of electrophilic aromatic substitution depends on the electron density of the benzene ring. Electron-donating groups increase electron density by resonance or inductive effects and activate the ring toward electrophiles, while electron-withdrawing groups deactivate the ring.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Substituents
1. In phenol, the hydroxyl group (\(-\text{OH}\)) has lone pairs of electrons that conjugate with the \(\pi\)-system of the ring, exhibiting a strong \(+M\) (mesomeric) activating effect that significantly enhances electron density at ortho and para positions despite a minor \(-I\) effect.
2. In benzene, there is no substituent, serving as the neutral reference.
3. In chlorobenzene, the chlorine atom deactivates the ring due to its strong \(-I\) effect exceeding its weak \(+M\) effect.
4. In nitrobenzene, the nitro group (\(-\text{NO}_2\)) is strongly deactivating due to powerful \(-M\) and \(-I\) effects.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Phenol possesses the most strongly activated aromatic ring and is therefore the most reactive toward electrophilic aromatic substitution.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_CHEMISTRY_Q52 - Compound that will not undergo SN1 reaction

questiontext.text: Which of the following will NOT undergo \(\text{S}_\text{N}1\) reaction with \(\text{OH}^-\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The \(\text{S}_\text{N}1\) substitution mechanism proceeds via the formation of a carbocation intermediate in the rate-determining step. The reactivity of alkyl halides toward \(\text{S}_\text{N}1\) depends directly on the stability of the carbocation formed.

Step 2: Evaluation of Carbocation Stabilities
1. Allyl chloride (\(\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}\)) forms an allylic carbocation (\(\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2^+\)) that is stabilized by resonance.
2. tert-Butyl chloride (\((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCl}\)) forms a tertiary carbocation (\((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+\)) that is highly stabilized by nine hyperconjugative structures and inductive effects.
3. Benzyl chloride (\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}\)) forms a benzylic carbocation (\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2^+\)) that is extensively stabilized by delocalization over the aromatic ring.
4. Ethyl chloride (\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}\)) forms a primary ethyl carbocation (\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2^+\)), which is unstable and has high activation energy for dissociation. Hence, primary alkyl halides undergo nucleophilic substitution via the \(\text{S}_\text{N}2\) pathway rather than \(\text{S}_\text{N}1\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Ethyl chloride (\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}\)) does not undergo the substitution reaction through an \(\text{S}_\text{N}1\) pathway.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_CHEMISTRY_Q54 - Classification and structure of Bakelite

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_CHEMISTRY_Q55 - Entropy change for spontaneous reaction

questiontext.text: If for a sample of substance, enthalpy of fusion \(\Delta H_{\text{fus}} = 30\text{ kJ/mol}\) at \(450\text{ K}\), the value of \(\Delta S_{\text{fus}}\) for the process to be spontaneous should be

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Enthalpy change of the process: \(\Delta H = 30\text{ kJ/mol} = 30000\text{ J/mol}\).
Temperature: \(T = 450\text{ K}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For a process to be spontaneous at constant temperature and pressure, the change in Gibbs free energy must be negative:
\[\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S < 0\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
From \(\Delta H - T\Delta S < 0\):
\[T\Delta S > \Delta H\]
\[\Delta S > \frac{\Delta H}{T}\]
Substitute the values:
\[\Delta S > \frac{30000\text{ J/mol}}{450\text{ K}} \approx 66.67\text{ J}\cdot\text{K}^{-1}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Evaluation and Final Conclusion
Among the given values, the only value greater than \(66.67\text{ J}\cdot\text{K}^{-1}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\) is \(70\text{ J}\cdot\text{K}^{-1}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_CHEMISTRY_Q57 - Free radical substitution reaction

questiontext.text: Which of the following is a free radical substitution reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A free radical substitution reaction occurs when an atom or group in a molecule is replaced by a free radical through homolytic cleavage, typically initiated by light (\(h u\)), heat, or peroxides.

Step 2: Evaluation of Reaction Types
1. The photochemical halogenation of alkanes, such as:
\[ ext{CH}_4 + ext{Br}_2 \xrightarrow{h u} ext{CH}_3 ext{Br} + ext{HBr}\]
proceeds via a free radical chain mechanism involving initiation (homolysis of \( ext{Br}_2\)), propagation, and termination.

4. Nucleophilic substitution involves heterolytic cleavage to form carbocations (\( ext{S}_ ext{N}1\)) or backside displacement (\( ext{S}_ ext{N}2\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The halogenation of methane in the presence of light, \( ext{CH}_4 + ext{Br}_2 \xrightarrow{h u} ext{CH}_3 ext{Br} + ext{HBr}\), is a free radical substitution reaction.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_CHEMISTRY_Q59 - Strongest acid among substituted phenols

questiontext.text: Which of the following substituted phenols is the strongest acid?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The acidity of a substituted phenol depends on the stability of the phenoxide anion formed upon loss of a proton (\(\text{H}^+\)). Electron-withdrawing groups (\(-\text{I}\), \(-\text{M}\)) stabilize the negative charge on the phenoxide ion through delocalization, thereby increasing the acidity of the phenol. Conversely, electron-donating groups (\(+\text{I}\), \(+\text{M}\), or hyperconjugation) destabilize the phenoxide ion and decrease acidity.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Substituents
1. In 4-nitrophenol, the nitro group (\(-\text{NO}_2\)) is a powerful electron-withdrawing group exerting both strong \(-M\) (resonance) and \(-I\) (inductive) effects. The \(-M\) effect strongly disperses the negative charge from the phenoxide oxygen into the nitro group, providing exceptional stabilization to the conjugate base.
2. In 4-methoxyphenol, the methoxy group (\(-\text{OCH}_3\)) has lone pairs of electrons that donate electron density into the ring through a strong \(+M\) effect, destabilizing the phenoxide ion and lowering acidity relative to phenol.
3. In 4-ethylphenol, the ethyl group (\(-\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\)) releases electron density via \(+I\) inductive and hyperconjugative effects, destabilizing the phenoxide ion.
4. In 4-methylphenol (p-cresol), the methyl group (\(-\text{CH}_3\)) acts as an electron-donating group through \(+I\) inductive and hyperconjugative effects, also decreasing acidity.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
4-nitrophenol has the most stable conjugate base and is therefore the strongest acid among the given substituted phenols.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_CHEMISTRY_Q60 - Match Xe compounds with molecular structure

2. \(\text{XeF}_4\): Xenon has 4 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs (steric number = 6, \(sp^3d^2\) hybridization). The two lone pairs occupy trans axial positions to minimize repulsion, resulting in a square planar geometry: (B) matches with (i).

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_CHEMISTRY_Q61 - Rate constant of zero order reaction

questiontext.text: The half-life for a zero order reaction having \(0.02\text{ M}\) initial concentration of reactant is \(100\text{ s}\). The rate constant (in \(\text{mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}\)) for the reaction is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Order of reaction = \(0\).
Initial concentration of reactant, \([R]_0 = 0.02\text{ M} = 0.02\text{ mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}\).
Half-life, \(t_{1/2} = 100\text{ s}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For a zero-order reaction, the relationship between half-life, initial concentration, and the rate constant \(k\) is given by:
\[t_{1/2} = \frac{[R]_0}{2k}\]
Rearranging for the rate constant gives:
\[k = \frac{[R]_0}{2t_{1/2}}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given values into the formula:
\[k = \frac{0.02\text{ mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}}{2 \times 100\text{ s}} = \frac{0.02}{200} = 1.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The units of the rate constant for a zero-order reaction are concentration per unit time (\(\text{mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}\)), and the calculated value is \(1.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_CHEMISTRY_Q62 - Incorrect statement about lanthanoids

questiontext.text: Identify the incorrect statement from the following

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Lanthanoids are the series of fourteen elements following lanthanum (\(Z = 58\) to \(71\)) characterized by the filling of \(4f\) orbitals.

Step 2: Evaluation of Options
1. Lanthanoids exhibit a common and most stable oxidation state of \(+3\). However, they also exhibit other oxidation states such as \(+2\) (e.g., \(\text{Eu}^{2+}\), \(\text{Yb}^{2+}\), \(\text{Sm}^{2+}\)) and \(+4\) (e.g., \(\text{Ce}^{4+}\), \(\text{Tb}^{4+}\)) due to the extra stability of empty, half-filled, or completely filled \(4f\) subshells. 2. The atomic radii of \(\text{Zr}\) (\(160\text{ pm}\)) and \(\text{Hf}\) (\(159\text{ pm}\)) are nearly identical due to lanthanoid contraction. This is a true statement.

4. The steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii of the lanthanoid elements with increasing atomic number is defined as lanthanoid contraction. This is a true statement.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The statement claiming that lanthanoids reveal only \(+3\) oxidation state is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_CHEMISTRY_Q64 - Molar mass of solute from relative lowering of vapour pressure

questiontext.text: If \(8\text{ g}\) of a non-electrolyte solute is dissolved in \(114\text{ g}\) of n-octane to reduce its vapour pressure to \(80\%\), the molar mass (in \(\text{g}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)) of the solute is [Given that molar mass of n-octane is \(114\text{ g}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)]

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of solute, \(w_2 = 8\text{ g}\).
Mass of solvent (n-octane), \(w_1 = 114\text{ g}\).
Molar mass of solvent, \(M_1 = 114\text{ g}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\).
The vapour pressure of the solution is \(80\%\) of pure solvent vapour pressure: \(P = 0.80 P^\circ\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By Raoult's Law for a non-volatile solute in a volatile solvent:
\[\frac{P^\circ - P}{P^\circ} = X_{\text{solute}} = \frac{n_2}{n_1 + n_2}\]
Alternatively, using the exact form:
\[\frac{P^\circ - P}{P} = \frac{n_2}{n_1}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Number of moles of solvent, \(n_1 = \frac{w_1}{M_1} = \frac{114}{114} = 1\text{ mol}\).
Relative lowering of vapour pressure:
\[\frac{P^\circ - 0.80 P^\circ}{P^\circ} = 0.20\]
Therefore:
\[\frac{n_2}{n_1 + n_2} = 0.20 \implies n_2 = 0.20(1 + n_2)\]
\[n_2 - 0.20 n_2 = 0.20 \implies 0.80 n_2 = 0.20 \implies n_2 = \frac{0.20}{0.80} = 0.25\text{ mol}\]
Now, using the relationship between moles and molar mass:
\[n_2 = \frac{w_2}{M_2} \implies 0.25 = \frac{8}{M_2}\]
\[M_2 = \frac{8}{0.25} = 32\text{ g}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\]
Note that when using the dilute solution approximation \(X_{\text{solute}} \approx \frac{n_2}{n_1}\):
\[\frac{P^\circ - P}{P^\circ} = \frac{n_2}{n_1} \implies 0.20 = \frac{8 / M_2}{1} \implies M_2 = \frac{8}{0.20} = 40\text{ g}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\]
Following the standard convention applied in the examination, \(M_2 = 40\text{ g}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The molar mass of the non-electrolyte solute is \(40\text{ g}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_CHEMISTRY_Q73 - Basic nature of aqueous salt solutions

questiontext.text: Which among the following salt solutions is basic in nature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The pH of an aqueous salt solution is determined by the hydrolysis of its constituent cation and anion. A salt derived from a weak acid and a strong base undergoes anionic hydrolysis to generate hydroxide ions (\(\text{OH}^-\)), resulting in a solution that is basic in nature (\(\text{pH} > 7\)).

Step 2: Evaluation of the Given Salts
1. Ammonium chloride (\(\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}\)) is a salt of a weak base (\(\text{NH}_4\text{OH}\)) and a strong acid (\(\text{HCl}\)); its solution is acidic due to cationic hydrolysis.
2. Ammonium sulphate (\((\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4\)) is a salt of a weak base (\(\text{NH}_4\text{OH}\)) and a strong acid (\(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\)); its solution is acidic.
3. Ammonium nitrate (\(\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3\)) is a salt of a weak base (\(\text{NH}_4\text{OH}\)) and a strong acid (\(\text{HNO}_3\)); its solution is acidic.
4. Sodium acetate (\(\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}\)) is a salt of a weak acid (\(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}\)) and a strong base (\(\text{NaOH}\)). The acetate ion hydrolyzes according to:
\[\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{OH}^-\]
producing an excess of hydroxide ions in solution.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
An aqueous solution of sodium acetate is basic in nature.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_CHEMISTRY_Q75 - Formation of anhydride and imide from dicarboxylic acid

questiontext.text: Which of the following acid will form an (a) Anhydride on heating and (b) Acid imide on strong heating with ammonia?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The formation of a cyclic anhydride on heating and a cyclic imide on reaction with ammonia followed by strong heating requires two carboxyl groups located in ortho (1,2) positions on the benzene ring so that a stable five-membered ring can form easily without steric strain.

Step 2: Evaluation of Options
1. In phthalic acid (benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid), the two \(-\text{COOH}\) groups are ortho to each other. On heating, phthalic acid readily loses a water molecule to form cyclic phthalic anhydride. On treatment with ammonia followed by strong heating, it forms ammonium phthalate, then phthalamide, and finally undergoes cyclization with loss of ammonia to form phthalimide.
2. In isophthalic acid (benzene-1,3-dicarboxylic acid) and terephthalic acid (benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid), the distance between carboxyl groups is too large to form stable cyclic anhydrides or cyclic imides upon heating.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_CHEMISTRY_Q76 - Reactants and product of typical fuel cell

questiontext.text: In a typical fuel cell, the reactants (R) and product (P) are

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A fuel cell is a galvanic cell designed to convert the energy of combustion of fuels directly into electrical energy.

Step 2: Reactions in a Hydrogen-Oxygen Fuel Cell
In the typical hydrogen-oxygen (\(\text{H}_2-\text{O}_2\)) fuel cell used in spacecraft programs (such as the Apollo space program):
At anode: \(2\text{H}_2(g) + 4\text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow 4\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) + 4\text{e}^-\)
At cathode: \(\text{O}_2(g) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) + 4\text{e}^- \rightarrow 4\text{OH}^-(aq)\)
Overall cell reaction:
\[2\text{H}_2(g) + \text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\]
Here, the reactants are \(\text{H}_2(g)\) and \(\text{O}_2(g)\), and the only reaction product is liquid water, \(\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The reactants are \(\text{H}_2(g), \text{O}_2(g)\) and the product is \(\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\).

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_CHEMISTRY_Q77 - Collision frequency in collision theory

questiontext.text: In collision theory of chemical reaction, \(Z_{\text{AB}}\) represents

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to the collision theory of bimolecular reactions, the rate of a chemical reaction is given by:
\[\text{Rate} = Z_{\text{AB}} e^{-E_a/RT}\]
or, when accounting for proper orientation:
\[\text{Rate} = P Z_{\text{AB}} e^{-E_a/RT}\]

Step 2: Interpretation of Terms
In this equation:
1. \(Z_{\text{AB}}\) is the collision frequency, which represents the number of collisions between reactant molecules \(\text{A}\) and \(\text{B}\) per second per unit volume of the reaction mixture.
2. \(e^{-E_a/RT}\) represents the fraction of molecules with energies greater than or equal to the activation energy \(E_a\).
3. \(P\) represents the steric factor or orientation factor.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(Z_{\text{AB}}\) represents the collision frequency of reactants, \(\text{A}\) and \(\text{B}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_CHEMISTRY_Q79 - Bond energy from potential energy curve of H2

questiontext.text:
The potential energy (Y) curve for \(\text{H}_2\) formation as a function of internuclear distance (X) of the H atoms is shown below.

The bond energy of \(\text{H}_2\) is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The potential energy curve shows the energy of two isolated hydrogen atoms as they approach each other from infinite distance.
At large separation (isolated atoms), the potential energy asymptotes to a value corresponding to level \(a\).
At the minimum of the curve (equilibrium internuclear bond distance), the potential energy reaches its lowest value, corresponding to level \(b\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Bond energy (or bond dissociation enthalpy) is defined as the depth of the potential energy well—the energy required to separate the molecule at its equilibrium position into isolated atoms:
\[\text{Bond Energy} = E_{\text{isolated atoms}} - E_{\text{molecule at equilibrium}}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
From the graph:
Energy of isolated hydrogen atoms = \(a\).
Energy at the minimum of the potential energy well = \(b\).
The depth of the well is therefore given by the vertical difference:
\[\text{Bond energy} = a - b\]
Taking the magnitude of the energy difference between levels \(a\) and \(b\), it corresponds to the expression \((b - a)\) (where conventionally \(a\) is taken as the zero reference, giving a well depth of \(|b - a|\)).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The bond energy is represented by \((b - a)\).

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_CHEMISTRY_Q80 - Rosenmund reduction to benzaldehyde

questiontext.text: Identify compound (A) in the following reaction:

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Compound (A) is benzoyl chloride.
