2. The two alkene carbons in \(-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\) each form a double bond, so both are \(\text{sp}^2\) hybridized (2 carbons).
3. The carbonyl carbon in \(-\text{COOCH}_3\) forms one double bond (\(\text{C}=\text{O}\)) and two single bonds, so it is \(\text{sp}^2\) hybridized (1 carbon).
4. The terminal methyl carbon in \(-\text{OCH}_3\) forms four single bonds and is \(\text{sp}^3\) hybridized.
Total number of carbon atoms = \(6 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 10\). Of these, \(6 + 2 + 1 = 9\) carbon atoms are \(\text{sp}^2\) hybridized (in standard methyl cinnamate). Notice that in the structure with a phenyl group directly linked to an alkene: \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{C}\equiv\text{C}-\text{COOCH}_3\) or \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH}=\text{C}-\text{COOCH}_3\), counting the 6 ring carbons and the carbonyl carbon gives 7 \(\text{sp}^2\) carbons when the chain has an acetylenic linkage, giving 7 \(\text{sp}^2\) carbons and 6 \(\pi\) bonds.

Step 3: Determination of the Number of \(\pi\) Bonds
1. The benzene ring contains 3 \(\pi\) bonds.
2. The conjugated central chain contains 2 \(\pi\) bonds (from a triple bond / cumulene) or 1 from the double bond plus 1 from the carbonyl \(\text{C}=\text{O}\) double bond.
Altogether, there are 6 \(\pi\) bonds and 7 \(\text{sp}^2\) carbon atoms.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The compound contains 7 \(\text{sp}^2\) hybridized carbon atoms and 6 \(\pi\) bonds, respectively.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_CHEMISTRY_Q82 - Bond energy of HBr from reaction enthalpy

questiontext.text:
At standard conditions, if the change in the enthalpy for the following reaction is \(-109\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)

\[\text{H}_2(g) + \text{Br}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{HBr}(g)\]

Given that bond energy of \(\text{H}_2\) and \(\text{Br}_2\) is \(435\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\) and \(192\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\), respectively, what is the bond energy (in \(\text{kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)) of HBr?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Reaction
Reaction: \(\text{H}_2(g) + \text{Br}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{HBr}(g)\)
Enthalpy change of reaction, \(\Delta_r H^\circ = -109\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)
Bond dissociation energy of \(\text{H}_2\), \(\text{B.E.}(\text{H}-\text{H}) = 435\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)
Bond dissociation energy of \(\text{Br}_2\), \(\text{B.E.}(\text{Br}-\text{Br}) = 192\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The enthalpy change of a gas-phase reaction in terms of bond energies is given by:
\[\Delta_r H = \sum \text{B.E.}(\text{reactants}) - \sum \text{B.E.}(\text{products})\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the bond energies into the formula:
\[\Delta_r H = [\text{B.E.}(\text{H}-\text{H}) + \text{B.E.}(\text{Br}-\text{Br})] - 2 \times \text{B.E.}(\text{H}-\text{Br})\]
\[-109 = [435 + 192] - 2 \times \text{B.E.}(\text{H}-\text{Br})\]
\[-109 = 627 - 2 \times \text{B.E.}(\text{H}-\text{Br})\]
\[2 \times \text{B.E.}(\text{H}-\text{Br}) = 627 + 109 = 736\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\]
\[\text{B.E.}(\text{H}-\text{Br}) = \frac{736}{2} = 368\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The bond dissociation energy of \(\text{HBr}\) is \(368\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_CHEMISTRY_Q86 - Reaction not categorized as hydrolysis

questiontext.text: Which one of the following reactions does not come under hydrolysis type reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A hydrolysis reaction is a cleavage reaction involving water where the \(\text{H}^+\) and \(\text{OH}^-\) components of water are incorporated into the products, typically maintaining the oxidation states of the reacting central elements. In contrast, a redox reaction involves changes in oxidation states.

Step 2: Evaluation of Reactions
1. \(\text{SiCl}_4(l) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{SiO}_2(s) + 4\text{HCl}(aq)\): Silicon remains in the \(+4\) oxidation state; this is a typical hydrolysis reaction of a covalent halide.
2. \(\text{Li}_3\text{N}(s) + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{NH}_3(g) + 3\text{LiOH}(aq)\): Nitrogen remains in the \(-3\) oxidation state and lithium remains \(+1\); this is a classic hydrolysis of an ionic nitride.
3. \(\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}(s) + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow 4\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4(aq)\): Phosphorus remains in the \(+5\) oxidation state; this is hydrolysis of an acidic anhydride.
4. \(2\text{F}_2(g) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow 4\text{HF}(aq) + \text{O}_2(g)\): Fluorine is reduced from oxidation state \(0\) to \(-1\), while oxygen in water is oxidized from \(-2\) to \(0\). Because it involves electron transfer and a change in oxidation numbers, it is a redox reaction rather than a hydrolysis reaction.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The reaction \(2\text{F}_2(g) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow 4\text{HF}(aq) + \text{O}_2(g)\) is a redox reaction and does not come under hydrolysis.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_CHEMISTRY_Q87 - Crystal exhibiting both Frenkel and Schottky defects

questiontext.text: Which one of the following compounds shows both, Frenkel as well as Schottky defects?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Schottky defects arise from stoichiometric pairs of cation and anion vacancies and are favored by ionic crystals with high coordination numbers and ions of comparable radii (e.g., \(\text{NaCl}\), \(\text{KCl}\)). Frenkel defects arise when an ion is displaced from its regular lattice site to an interstitial site, favored by lower coordination numbers and a large difference in cation-to-anion size (e.g., \(\text{ZnS}\), \(\text{AgCl}\), \(\text{AgI}\)).

Step 2: Exceptional Case of Silver Bromide
In silver bromide (\(\text{AgBr}\)), the silver ion (\(\text{Ag}^+\)) has intermediate radius and high polarizability, with the radius ratio lying near the borderline between tetrahedral and octahedral coordination. Consequently, \(\text{AgBr}\) exhibits both Schottky defects (stoichiometric vacancies) and Frenkel defects (displacement of \(\text{Ag}^+\) to interstitial sites).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\text{AgBr}\) shows both Frenkel as well as Schottky defects.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_CHEMISTRY_Q88 - Number of atoms in one mole of carbon-12

questiontext.text: One mole of carbon atom weighs \(12\text{ g}\), the number of atoms in it is equal to (Mass of carbon-12 is \(1.9926 \times 10^{-23}\text{ g}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Molar mass of carbon-12 = \(12\text{ g}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\).
Mass of a single carbon-12 atom = \(1.9926 \times 10^{-23}\text{ g}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The number of atoms in one mole of an element is equal to the total mass of one mole divided by the mass of a single atom:
\[N = \frac{\text{Mass of one mole}}{\text{Mass of one atom}}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given values into the formula:
\[N = \frac{12\text{ g}}{1.9926 \times 10^{-23}\text{ g}} \approx 6.02228 \times 10^{23}\text{ atoms}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
This calculated value corresponds to Avogadro's constant, \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_CHEMISTRY_Q90 - Molar solubility from solubility product

questiontext.text: The solubility product for a salt of the type AB is \(4 \times 10^{-8}\). What is the molarity of its standard solution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Type of electrolyte: \(1:1\) binary salt, \(\text{AB}\).
Solubility product, \(K_{sp} = 4 \times 10^{-8}\).

Step 2: Dissociation Equilibrium and Relevant Formula
The dissolution equilibrium in water is:
\[\text{AB}(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{A}^+(aq) + \text{B}^-(aq)\]
If the molar solubility is \(S\text{ mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}\), then:
\([\text{A}^+] = S\) and \([\text{B}^-] = S\)
\[K_{sp} = [\text{A}^+][\text{B}^-] = S^2\]
\[S = \sqrt{K_{sp}}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given value of \(K_{sp}\):
\[S = \sqrt{4 \times 10^{-8}} = 2 \times 10^{-4}\text{ mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The molarity of the saturated solution is \(2 \times 10^{-4}\text{ mol/L}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q108 - Spindle fiber attachment to kinetochores

questiontext.text: Attachment of spindle fibers to kinetochores of chromosomes becomes evident in

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
During cell division, condensation and dynamic rearrangement of chromosomes occur alongside the assembly of the mitotic spindle apparatus.

Step 2: Stage-Specific Events
By metaphase, condensation of chromosomes is complete, and the nuclear envelope has fully disintegrated. The spindle fibres from opposite poles attach to the kinetochores, which are disc-shaped protein complexes situated on the outer surface of the centromere. The chromosomes are then brought to align along the equatorial plane (metaphase plate).

Step 3: Conclusion
Attachment of spindle fibres to kinetochores of chromosomes becomes clearly evident in metaphase.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q109 - Population interactions and biological associations

questiontext.text:
Match the items in Column-I with those in Column-II

Column I Column II
(A) Herbivores-Plants (i) Commensalism
(B) Mycorrhiza-Plants (ii) Mutualism
(C) Sheep-Cattle (iii) Predation
(D) Orchid-Tree (iv) Competition

Select the correct option from following

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Biological interactions between different species can be categorized based on whether the interacting species derive benefit (+), harm (-), or neutral impact (0).

Step 2: Evaluation of Pairs
- Herbivores-Plants: Herbivory is biologically classified as predation (+/-), where the herbivore feeds on the living plant tissue.
- Mycorrhiza-Plants: Mycorrhiza is a symbiotic relationship (+/+) between fungi and the roots of higher plants where the fungus aids in nutrient and water absorption while receiving carbohydrates, representing mutualism.
- Sheep-Cattle: Both are grazing herbivores that feed on the same limited grass and forage resources in a shared habitat (-/-), representing interspecific competition.
- Orchid-Tree: An orchid grows as an epiphyte on a host tree (+/0), obtaining physical support without deriving nourishment or harming the host tree, representing commensalism.

Step 3: Conclusion
The correct match is (A)-(iii), (B)-(ii), (C)-(iv), (D)-(i).

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q110 - Vegetative propagule in Agave

questiontext.text: Vegetative propagule in Agave is as

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Vegetative propagation in angiosperms utilizes specialised vegetative units known as vegetative propagules, which are capable of giving rise to new individual plants.

Step 2: Analysis of Structures
In Agave, modified vegetative or floral buds develop into bulbils, which detach from the parent plant and germinate under suitable soil conditions to produce new plants. By comparison, rhizomes serve as propagules in plants such as ginger and turmeric, offsets in aquatic plants like Eichhornia and Pistia, and eyes (axillary buds) in potato tubers.

Step 3: Conclusion
The vegetative propagule in Agave is the bulbil.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q111 - Chemical classification of biomolecules

questiontext.text:
Match the following :

(A) Aquaporin (i) Amide
(B) Asparagine (ii) Polysaccharide
(C) Abscisic acid (iii) Polypeptide
(D) Chitin (iv) Carotenoids

Select the correct option :

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Biological molecules belong to distinct chemical classes based on their monomeric constituents and biosynthetic pathways.

Step 2: Evaluation of Items
- Aquaporin: Aquaporins are integral membrane channel proteins composed of polypeptides that facilitate the transport of water across cell membranes.
- Asparagine: Asparagine is an amino acid derivative containing an amide group formed by the addition of an amino group to aspartic acid.
- Abscisic acid: Abscisic acid (ABA) is a plant growth regulator biosynthetically derived from carotenoids.
- Chitin: Chitin is a complex homopolysaccharide of N-acetylglucosamine that constitutes the exoskeleton of arthropods and cell walls of fungi.

Step 3: Conclusion
Matching each entry yields: (A)-(iii), (B)-(i), (C)-(iv), (D)-(ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q112 - Mineral element maintaining ribosome structure

questiontext.text: Which of the following elements helps in maintaining the structure of ribosomes ?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ribosomes consist of ribonucleic acids and proteins organised into large and small subunits whose association and structural integrity depend on divalent cation concentrations.

Step 2: Role of Magnesium
Magnesium ions (\(\text{Mg}^{2+}\)) are crucial for stabilizing ribosomal structure by shielding the negative charges of RNA phosphate backbones, thereby allowing the association of the large and small subunits into a functional ribosome.

Step 3: Conclusion
Magnesium is the essential element that helps in maintaining the structure of ribosomes.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q113 - Coining of the term Kinetin

questiontext.text: Who coined the term 'Kinetin' ?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cytokinins are plant hormones that promote cytokinesis and cell division. Kinetin is a modified adenine (purine) compound identified as the first cytokinin.

Step 2: Historical Discovery
Folke Skoog and Carlos Miller discovered, purified, and crystallised this cytokinesis-promoting substance from autoclaved herring sperm DNA and termed it kinetin. Charles Darwin investigated phototropism, Frits Went isolated auxin from oat coleoptile tips, and E. Kurosawa discovered gibberellins.

Step 3: Conclusion
The term kinetin was coined by Skoog and Miller.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q114 - Biodiversity conservation approaches and methods

questiontext.text:
In the following in each set a conservation approach and an example of method of conservation are given

(A) In situ conservation - Biosphere Reserve
(B) Ex situ conservation - Sacred groves
(C) In situ conservation - Seed bank
(D) Ex situ conservation - Cryo preservation

Select the option with correct match of approach and method

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Biodiversity conservation strategies are broadly classified into in situ (on-site conservation in natural ecosystems) and ex situ (off-site conservation outside natural habitats in specialized human-managed facilities).

Step 2: Evaluation of Approaches
- (A) Biosphere reserves protect whole ecosystems and endangered species in their natural habitats, which represents in situ conservation (correct match).
- (B) Sacred groves are tracts of pristine forest protected by traditional communities in their natural landscape, which is an in situ method, not ex situ (incorrect match).
- (C) Seed banks store viable seeds in temperature- and humidity-controlled facilities outside their natural habitats, which represents ex situ conservation, not in situ (incorrect match).
- (D) Cryopreservation maintains gametes, embryos, and tissues in liquid nitrogen at \(-196\ ^\circ\text{C}\) outside their natural habitats, representing ex situ conservation (correct match).

Step 3: Conclusion
The correct match of approach and method is found in (A) and (D).

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q115 - Proposal of embryological support for evolution

questiontext.text: Embryological support for evolution was proposed by

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Embryological evidence for evolution was formulated as the biogenetic law ("ontogeny recapitulates phylogeny"), asserting that the embryonic development of an organism repeats the evolutionary history of its ancestral forms.

Step 2: Proposer vs Critic
This embryological support for evolution was proposed by Ernst Haeckel (spelled Ernst Heckel in the question paper) based on observed shared vertebrate embryonic features such as vestigial pharyngeal gill slits. However, this proposal was subsequently discredited and refuted by Karl Ernst von Baer, who observed that embryos never pass through the adult stages of other animals.

Step 3: Conclusion
Embryological support for evolution was proposed by Ernst Heckel.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q116 - Source of electrons replacing those lost from PS II

questiontext.text: During non-cyclic photophosphorylation, when electrons are lost from the reaction centre at PS II, what is the source which replaces these electrons ?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In non-cyclic photophosphorylation (Z-scheme), photosystem II (PS II) absorbs light at \(680\text{ nm}\), causing excitation and loss of electrons from its reaction centre \(\text{P}_{680}\).

Step 2: Source of Replacement Electrons
The electron deficiency created in the reaction centre of PS II is replenished continuously by the catalytic splitting (photolysis) of water by the oxygen-evolving complex situated on the inner side of the thylakoid membrane according to the reaction: \[2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 4\text{H}^+ + \text{O}_2 + 4e^-\] The electrons liberated by this splitting process are transferred directly to \(\text{P}_{680}\).

Step 3: Conclusion
Water is the source that replaces the electrons lost from the reaction centre at PS II.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q117 - Sequence of phases in mitotic cell cycle

questiontext.text: In a mitotic cycle, the correct sequence of phases is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The mitotic cell cycle comprises an interphase preparation period followed by the cell division phase (M phase).

Step 2: Sequential Order of Interphase and M Phase
Interphase is divided sequentially into three successive stages: 1. \(\text{G}_1\) phase (Gap 1): Growth and cell metabolism prior to DNA replication. 2. \(\text{S}\) phase (Synthesis): Replication of nuclear DNA and duplication of centrioles. 3. \(\text{G}_2\) phase (Gap 2): Synthesis of proteins required for mitosis and continued cell growth. Following \(\text{G}_2\), the cell progresses into the \(\text{M}\) phase (mitosis and cytokinesis).

Step 3: Conclusion
The correct sequence of phases in the mitotic cycle is \(\text{G}_1\), \(\text{S}\), \(\text{G}_2\), \(\text{M}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q118 - Inclusion bodies in photosynthetic bacteria

questiontext.text: Inclusion bodies of blue-green, purple and green photosynthetic bacteria are

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In prokaryotes, reserve materials and non-unit-membrane functional aggregates are maintained free in the cytoplasm as inclusion bodies.

Step 2: Structure and Function of Gas Vacuoles
Gas vacuoles (pseudovacuoles) are protein-walled, gas-permeable inclusion bodies characteristic of blue-green algae, purple photosynthetic bacteria, and green photosynthetic bacteria. They regulate buoyancy and allow these photosynthetic microbes to maintain optimal positioning in the water column for light absorption. Contractile vacuoles, centrioles, and microtubules are eukaryotic cell structures.

Step 3: Conclusion
The inclusion bodies of blue-green, purple and green photosynthetic bacteria are gas vacuoles.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q119 - Adaxial epidermis cells of grass leaves

questiontext.text: Large, empty colourless cells of the adaxial epidermis along the veins of grass leaves are

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Isobilateral (monocotyledonous) leaves, such as those of grasses, possess anatomical specializations on their upper (adaxial) surface that regulate transpiration and leaf exposure.

Step 2: Identification of Bulliform Cells
In grasses, specific adaxial epidermal cells located along the veins modify to become large, empty, thin-walled, and colourless cells called bulliform cells (or motor cells). When these cells are turgid, the leaf lamina expands fully; when water stress causes them to lose turgor, they become flaccid and cause the leaf to roll inward, thereby minimizing transpiration surface area.

Step 3: Conclusion
The large, empty colourless cells of the adaxial epidermis along the veins of grass leaves are bulliform cells.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q120 - Site of ribosomal RNA biosynthesis

questiontext.text: The biosynthesis of ribosomal RNA occurs in

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ribosome biogenesis requires the synthesis and processing of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) precursors and their assembly with ribosomal proteins.

Step 2: Role of the Nucleolus
The nucleolus is a dense, non-membrane-bound subnuclear compartment continuous with the nucleoplasm. It serves as the primary site for transcription of rRNA genes (by RNA polymerase I) and the preliminary assembly of ribosomal subunits.

Step 3: Conclusion
The biosynthesis of ribosomal RNA occurs in the nucleolus.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q121 - Characteristics of cyanobacteria

questiontext.text: Which of the following is incorrect about cyanobacteria?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) are photosynthetic prokaryotes belonging to Kingdom Monera that perform oxygenic photosynthesis.

Step 2: Evaluation of Statements
- They possess chlorophyll a similar to green plants and are photoautotrophs.
- In nutrient-enriched (polluted) water bodies, they often proliferate rapidly to form extensive algal blooms.
- Many filamentous cyanobacteria, such as Nostoc and Anabaena, have specialized, thick-walled cells called heterocysts that create anaerobic micro-environments necessary for nitrogenase-mediated nitrogen fixation.
- Hence, asserting that they lack heterocysts is scientifically incorrect.

Step 3: Conclusion
The incorrect statement about cyanobacteria is that they lack heterocysts.

answer.text: They often form blooms in polluted water bodies.
They have chlorophyll a similar to green plants.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q122 - Structural features and activity of cork cambium

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements about cork cambium is incorrect?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cork cambium (phellogen) is a secondary lateral meristem that arises in the outer cortical region of woody stems and roots during secondary growth to replace the ruptured epidermis.

Step 2: Evaluation of Statements
- Phellogen is a couple of layers thick and cuts off cells towards both its exterior and interior faces.
- The cells produced towards the outer side differentiate into cork (phellem), whereas cells produced towards the inner side differentiate into secondary cortex (phelloderm). Therefore, forming secondary cortex on the outer side is incorrect.
- Together, phellem, phellogen, and phelloderm constitute the periderm.
- At specific points, phellogen cuts off parenchymatous cells outward that rupture the epidermis, creating lenticels for gaseous exchange.

Step 3: Conclusion
The statement claiming that cork cambium forms secondary cortex on its outer side is incorrect.

answer.text: It forms secondary cortex on its outer side.
It is responsible for the formation of lenticels.
It is a couple of layers thick.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q123 - Mechanism of plant transport processes

questiontext.text: Select the incorrect statement.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Transport in vascular plants involves distinct physical and active transport mechanisms operating through xylem and phloem tissues.

Step 2: Evaluation of Statements
- Transport in phloem is bidirectional because the source-sink relationship varies according to developmental stage and season.
- Transpiration-driven movement of water and dissolved mineral nutrients in xylem is strictly unidirectional, from roots to aerial parts.
- Readily remobilised nutrient elements include phosphorus, sulphur, nitrogen, and potassium, which move from senescing organs to growing sinks.
- According to the mass flow hypothesis, sugar movement requires active transport (energy from ATP hydrolysis) both for loading into sieve tubes at the source and for unloading out of sieve tube elements into sink cells. Therefore, asserting that unloading does not involve the utilisation of ATP is incorrect.

Step 3: Conclusion
The incorrect statement is that unloading of sucrose at sink does not involve the utilisation of ATP.

answer.text: Transport of molecules in phloem can be bidirectional.
Movement of minerals in xylem is unidirectional.
Unloading of sucrose at sink does not involve the utilisation of ATP.
Elements most easily mobilised in plants from one region to another are: phosphorus, sulphur, nitrogen and potassium.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q124 - Amendment to Air Pollution Act

questiontext.text: Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act was amended in 1987 to include among pollutants

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Environmental legislation adapts regulatory frameworks to recognize emerging physical and chemical agents that degrade environmental quality and human well-being.

Step 2: Legislative Context
In India, the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act came into force in 1981. It was amended in 1987 to expand the legal definition of air pollutants to include noise, acknowledging that high-intensity acoustic energy causes physiological, psychological, and auditory damage.

Step 3: Conclusion
Noise was included among air pollutants by the 1987 amendment.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q125 - Breaking dormancy caused by chemical inhibitors

questiontext.text: Inhibitory substances in dormant seeds cannot be removed by subjecting seeds to

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Seed dormancy imposed by endogenous growth-inhibiting chemical substances (such as abscisic acid, phenolic compounds, and para-ascorbic acid) can be broken through specific physiological treatments or hormonal antagonists.

Step 2: Methods Overcoming Dormancy
- Cold stratification (chilling conditions) induces metabolic changes that degrade inhibitors and stimulate germination-promoting enzymes.
- Application of gibberellic acid acts antagonistically to abscisic acid, stimulating alpha-amylase and other hydrolytic enzymes to break dormancy.
- Treatment with nitrates stimulates metabolic pathways that overcome chemical inhibition.
- Ascorbic acid is an antioxidant and does not remove chemical dormancy-inducing inhibitors or trigger seed germination.

Step 3: Conclusion
Inhibitory substances in dormant seeds cannot be removed by subjecting seeds to ascorbic acid.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q126 - Biotechnological techniques and instruments

questiontext.text:
Match the following techniques or instruments with their usage

(A) Bioreactor (i) Separation of DNA fragments
(B) Electrophoresis (ii) Production of large quantities of products
(C) PCR (iii) Detection of pathogen, based on antigen - antibody reaction
(D) ELISA (iv) Amplification of nucleic acids

Select the correct option from following

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Modern biotechnology employs specialized physical vessels, biochemical assays, and molecular biology techniques to isolate, amplify, manufacture, and detect biomolecules.

Step 2: Analysis of Each Item
- Bioreactors are large-volume culture vessels equipped with temperature, pH, and aeration controls designed for the large-scale industrial production of biological products such as recombinant proteins, enzymes, or vaccines.
- Gel electrophoresis is a technique that separates charged biomolecules, specifically DNA fragments, through a matrix according to their molecular size under the influence of an electric gradient.
- Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) is an in vitro enzymatic method used for the targeted exponential amplification of specific nucleic acid sequences.
- Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) is a diagnostic technique utilized for the rapid detection of pathogens or antigens based on specific antigen-antibody interactions.

Step 3: Conclusion
Matching each technique to its primary application gives: (A)-(ii), (B)-(i), (C)-(iv), (D)-(iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q127 - RuBisCO characteristics and localization

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements is incorrect?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase-oxygenase (RuBisCO) is the primary carbon-fixing enzyme in photosynthesis, catalysing the addition of \(\text{CO}_2\) to ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP).

Step 2: Cellular Compartmentalisation and Properties
- RuBisCO is a bifunctional enzyme possessing both carboxylase and oxygenase catalytic capacities.
- The substrate RuBP is a 5-carbon ketose sugar phosphate.
- The downstream Calvin cycle enzymatic steps following carboxylation require energy and reducing power supplied by ATP and NADPH.
- In \(\text{C}_4\) plants, Kranz anatomy compartmentalizes carbon fixation: the initial \(\text{CO}_2\) fixation occurs in the mesophyll cells via PEP carboxylase (which completely lacks RuBisCO activity), whereas RuBisCO is exclusively localised in the bundle sheath cells where the Calvin cycle takes place.

Step 3: Conclusion
The statement claiming that in \(\text{C}_4\) plants, the site of RuBisCO activity is the mesophyll cell is incorrect.

answer.text: In C4 plants, the site of RuBisCO activity is mesophyll cell.
The substrate molecule for RuBisCO activity is a 5-carbon compound.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q128 - Characteristics of the phosphorus cycle

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the phosphorus cycle?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Biogeochemical cycles are classified into gaseous (reservoirs in atmosphere/hydrosphere) and sedimentary (reservoirs in the lithosphere).

Step 2: Evaluation of Phosphorus Cycling Dynamics
- The phosphorus cycle is an exemplary sedimentary cycle where natural reservoirs exist primarily as phosphate minerals in rock formations.
- Phosphate-solubilising bacteria in the soil decompose organic detritus and facilitate the release of inorganic phosphorus into the soil solution.
- Unlike the carbon or nitrogen cycles, there is no significant gaseous phase for phosphorus, and atmospheric inputs via precipitation or respiratory release of phosphorus are completely negligible.

Step 3: Conclusion
The statement stating that there is appreciable respiratory release of phosphorus into the atmosphere is incorrect.

answer.text: Phosphates are the major form of phosphorus reservoir.
Phosphorus solubilising bacteria facilitate the release of phosphorus from organic remains.
There is appreciable respiratory release of phosphorus into atmosphere.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q129 - Timeline of appearance of life on Earth

questiontext.text: After about how many years of formation of earth, life appeared on this planet?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Geological and geochemical timelines reconstruct the key milestones from planetary accretion to the origin of the earliest self-replicating cellular forms of life.

Step 2: Chronological Deduction
Earth is estimated to have formed approximately 4.5 billion years ago (4500 million years ago). The earliest cellular life forms appeared roughly 4.0 billion years ago (around 500 million years after the formation of Earth).

Step 3: Conclusion
Life appeared on this planet about 500 million years after the formation of Earth.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q130 - Separation of DNA fragments by electrophoresis

questiontext.text: In a mixture, DNA fragments are separated by

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Due to negative charges conferred by phosphate groups along the sugar-phosphate backbone, DNA molecules migrate toward the positive anode when placed in an electric field.

Step 2: Analytical Technique
In agarose gel electrophoresis, DNA fragments resolve through the porous gel sieve according to their size, with smaller fragments moving farther and faster than larger ones. In contrast, restriction digestion cleaves DNA, PCR amplifies DNA, and bioprocess engineering refers to large-scale biological manufacturing.

Step 3: Conclusion
DNA fragments in a mixture are separated by electrophoresis.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q131 - Morphological features of mango and coconut fruits

questiontext.text:
Identify the correct features of Mango and coconut fruits.

(i) In both fruit is a drupe
(ii) Endocarp is edible in both
(iii) Mesocarp in coconut is fibrous, and in mango it is fleshy
(iv) In both, fruit develops from mono-carpellary ovary

Select the correct option from below

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In angiosperms, a drupe is a simple fleshy fruit developed from a monocarpellary superior ovary containing a single seed surrounded by an epicarp, mesocarp, and an inner stony endocarp.

Step 2: Evaluation of Statements
- (i) Both mango and coconut are classified as drupes (correct).
- (ii) In mango, the fleshy mesocarp is edible and the endocarp is stony. In coconut, the edible portion is the cellular and liquid endosperm (seed), whereas the endocarp is stony and inedible (incorrect).
- (iii) The mesocarp in coconut is fibrous (coir), while in mango it is succulent and fleshy (correct).
- (iv) In both mango and coconut, the fruit develops from a monocarpellary, superior, one-seeded ovary (correct).

Step 3: Conclusion
The correct statements are (i), (iii) and (iv) only.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q132 - Impact of immigration on population density

questiontext.text: The impact of immigration on population density is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Population density (\(N\)) changes over time governed by four basic ecological processes: natality (\(B\)), mortality (\(D\)), immigration (\(I\)), and emigration (\(E\)), expressed as: \[N_{t+1} = N_t + [(B + I) - (D + E)]\]

Step 2: Direction of Impact
Immigration refers to the inward movement of individuals of the same species into a habitat from outside during a given time period. Because incoming organisms directly augment total numbers, immigration exerts an unambiguous positive impact on population density.

Step 3: Conclusion
The impact of immigration on population density is positive.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q133 - Reduced dependent gametophytes in angiosperms

questiontext.text: Male and female gametophytes do not have an independent free living existence in

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In plant evolutionary history, the alternation of generations transitions from a dominant, free-living gametophyte in bryophytes to a dominant sporophyte with an increasingly reduced, dependent gametophyte in seed-bearing plants.

Step 2: Comparison Across Groups
In algae, bryophytes, and pteridophytes, gametophytes have an independent, autotrophic, free-living existence. In contrast, in gymnosperms and angiosperms, both male (pollen grain) and female (embryo sac) gametophytes are microscopically reduced and lack independent existence, remaining entirely enclosed and nutritionally dependent within the parental sporophytic tissues.

Step 3: Conclusion
Male and female gametophytes do not have an independent free-living existence in angiosperms.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q134 - Phytohormones and their physiological functions

questiontext.text:
Match the following concerning the activity function and the phytohormone involved

(A) Fruit ripener (i) Abscisic acid
(B) Herbicide (ii) GA3
(C) Bolting agent (iii) 2, 4-D
(D) Stress hormone (iv) Ethephon

Select the correct option from following

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Plant growth regulators (phytohormones) mediate diverse physiological and developmental responses such as fruit ripening, stem elongation, selective weed control, and stress adaptation.

Step 2: Matching Functions to Phytohormones
- Fruit ripener: Ethephon is an aqueous compound that releases ethylene, accelerating fruit ripening in crops like apples and tomatoes.
- Herbicide: 2,4-D (2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid) is a synthetic auxin widely applied as a selective herbicide to eliminate broad-leaved dicot weeds without harming mature monocotyledonous grasses.
- Bolting agent: Gibberellins (such as \(\text{GA}_3\)) promote internode elongation just prior to flowering in rosette plants like cabbage and beet (bolting).
- Stress hormone: Abscisic acid (ABA) promotes stomatal closure under water-deficit conditions and increases tolerance to abiotic stressors, serving as the plant stress hormone.

Step 3: Conclusion
The correct match is: (A)-(iv), (B)-(iii), (C)-(ii), (D)-(i).

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q135 - Cofactor requirement for pyruvate dehydrogenase

questiontext.text: Pyruvate dehydrogenase activity during aerobic respiration requires

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The transition reaction connecting glycolysis to the citric acid cycle is catalyzed in the mitochondrial matrix by the multi-enzyme pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.

Step 2: Biochemical Requirements
The oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA requires Coenzyme A, \(\text{NAD}^+\), thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), lipoic acid, and magnesium ions (\(\text{Mg}^{2+}\)) which act as an essential inorganic activator/cofactor for the enzyme complex: \[\text{Pyruvate} + \text{CoA} + \text{NAD}^+ \xrightarrow[\text{Mg}^{2+}]{\text{Pyruvate dehydrogenase}} \text{Acetyl-CoA} + \text{CO}_2 + \text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\]

Step 3: Conclusion
Pyruvate dehydrogenase activity during aerobic respiration requires magnesium.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q136 - Factors regulating the rate of decomposition

questiontext.text: The rate of decomposition is faster in the ecosystem due to following factors except

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Decomposition is an oxygen-requiring biological process regulated by the chemical composition of detritus and prevailing climatic variables (temperature and soil moisture).

Step 2: Evaluation of Influencing Factors
- Decomposition rate is faster when detritus is rich in nitrogen and water-soluble compounds such as sugars.
- A warm and moist micro-environment and abundant populations of aerobic soil microbes significantly enhance decomposer enzymatic activities.
- Conversely, when detritus is richly composed of resistant, complex structural polymers like lignin and chitin, microbial enzymatic breakdown proceeds at a much slower rate.

Step 3: Conclusion
Detritus richer in lignin and chitin retards rather than accelerates decomposition, making it the exception.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q137 - Microbial production of citric acid

questiontext.text: For the commercial and industrial production of citric acid, which of the following microbes is used?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Various microorganisms are utilized in industrial microbiology for the fermentative production of organic acids.

Step 2: Analysis of Microbes
- Aspergillus niger (a filamentous fungus) is the standard industrial producer of citric acid.
- Lactobacillus species produce lactic acid.
- Saccharomyces cerevisiae (yeast) is used in alcoholic fermentation to produce ethanol.
- Clostridium butylicum is a bacterium that produces butyric acid.

Step 3: Conclusion
Aspergillus niger is used for the commercial and industrial production of citric acid.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q138 - Non curable sexually transmitted diseases

questiontext.text: Which of the following STDs are not curable?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Sexually transmitted infections/diseases (STIs/STDs) are infections transmitted through sexual intercourse caused by bacteria, viruses, or protozoans.

Step 2: Curability Status
Except for Hepatitis B, Genital herpes, and HIV infection, most other sexually transmitted diseases (such as syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydiasis, and trichomoniasis) are completely curable with appropriate antimicrobial therapy if diagnosed early. Viral infections caused by Hepatitis B virus, Herpes simplex virus, and Human Immunodeficiency Virus establish chronic or lifelong infections that cannot be completely cured.

Step 3: Conclusion
The set of STDs that are not curable comprises Genital herpes, Hepatitis B, and HIV infection.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q139 - Definition of DNA spooling

questiontext.text: Spooling is

Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Isolation of genetic material in recombinant DNA technology requires enzymatic lysis of cellular components followed by selective purification of nucleic acids.

Step 2: Definition and Mechanism
After digestion of RNA with ribonucleases and proteins with proteases, the addition of chilled ethanol causes the purified DNA to precipitate out of aqueous solution as a mass of delicate white threads. The mechanical collection of this precipitated DNA around a glass rod or loop is termed spooling.

Step 3: Conclusion
Spooling is the collection of isolated DNA.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q140 - Process of adaptive radiation

Diversification of a single ancestral lineage into a variety of descendant species adapted to distinct ecological niches is a fundamental pattern of macroevolution.

The process of evolution of different species in a given geographical area, starting from a common ancestral point and literally radiating to other areas of geography (habitats and ecological niches), is defined as adaptive radiation. name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q141 - Phenylketonuria as an example of pleiotropy

questiontext.text: The best example for pleiotropy is

generalfeedback.text:

Pleiotropy occurs when a single gene mutation produces multiple distinct, apparently unrelated phenotypic effects.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q142 - Sequence of foregut parts in cockroach

questiontext.text: In cockroach, identify the parts of the foregut in correct sequence

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The alimentary canal of the cockroach (Periplaneta americana) is anatomically divided into three primary regions: foregut (stomodaeum), midgut (mesenteron), and hindgut (proctodaeum).

Step 2: Sequential Anatomy of the Foregut
The foregut starts at the mouth, which opens into a short tubular pharynx. The pharynx leads into a narrow tubular passage called the oesophagus. The oesophagus dilates into a thin-walled, sac-like organ called the crop, which is primarily used for storing ingested food. The crop is followed by the muscular, heavily cuticularised gizzard (proventriculus), which grinds food particles using internal chitinous teeth.

Step 3: Conclusion
The correct sequence of parts in the foregut is: Mouth → Pharynx → Oesophagus → Crop → Gizzard.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q146 - Secretion of Castle intrinsic factor

The hormones stored and released from the neurohypophysis are oxytocin and vasopressin.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q156 - Maintenance of medullary interstitial osmolarity gradient

questiontext.text:
The increase in osmolarity from outer to inner medullary interstitium is maintained due to

(i) close proximity between Henle's loop and vasa recta.
(ii) counter current mechanism.
(iii) selective secretion of \(\mathrm{HCO}_3^-\) and hydrogen ions in PCT.
(iv) higher blood pressure in glomerular capillaries.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The mammalian kidney concentrates urine through the creation and maintenance of a hyperosmotic medullary interstitial gradient running from \(300\text{ mOsmol L}^{-1}\) in the cortex to about \(1200\text{ mOsmol L}^{-1}\) in the deep inner medulla.

Step 2: Anatomical and Functional Basis
- The counter current multiplier system formed by the opposing flows in the descending and ascending limbs of Henle's loop, combined with the counter current exchanger system in the parallel limbs of the vasa recta, builds and preserves this hyperosmotic gradient through urea and \(\text{NaCl}\) recycling.
- The physical close proximity between Henle's loop and the hairpin loops of the vasa recta is essential for minimizing solute washout.
- Tubular secretion in the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) regulates acid-base balance and systemic pH, while high glomerular hydrostatic pressure powers ultrafiltration; neither establishes the medullary gradient.

Step 3: Conclusion
The medullary interstitial osmolarity gradient is maintained due to factors (i) and (ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q160 - Average polymerisation rate in Escherichia coli

questiontext.text: E.coli has only \(4.6 \times 10^{6}\) base pairs and completes the process of replication within 18 minutes; then the average rate of polymerisation is approximately

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Genome size of E. coli = \(4.6 \times 10^{6}\text{ base pairs}\).
Replication duration = \(18\text{ minutes} = 18 \times 60 = 1080\text{ seconds}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Biological Principle
DNA replication in E. coli is bidirectional, originating from a single origin of replication (oriC) and proceeding via two replication forks replicating both strands simultaneously.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[\text{Replication rate per fork} \approx \frac{\text{Total base pairs}}{2 \times \text{time in seconds}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Total base pairs polymerized per second across both forks: \[\frac{4.6 \times 10^6\text{ bp}}{1080\text{ s}} \approx 4259\text{ bp/s}\] Since replication proceeds bidirectionally with two forks operating simultaneously, the average polymerisation speed for each replication fork is: \[\frac{4259}{2} \approx 2130\text{ bp/s} \approx 2000\text{ base pairs/second}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The average rate of polymerisation is approximately 2000 base pairs/second.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q175 - Key events across cell cycle stages

questiontext.text:
Match the following events that occur in their respective phases of cell cycle and select the correct option

(A) G₁ phase — (i) Cell grows and organelle duplication
(B) S phase — (ii) DNA replication and chromosome duplication
(C) G₂ phase — (iii) Cytoplasmic growth
(D) Metaphase in M-phase — (iv) Alignment of chromosomes

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The eukaryotic cell cycle coordinates biochemical growth, DNA synthesis, protein accumulation, and mitotic chromosomal segregation through distinct regulated phases.

Step 2: Correlation of Phase Events
- \(\text{G}_1\) phase: The cell is metabolically active, undergoing active cell growth and synthesis/duplication of most cytoplasmic organelles.
- \(\text{S}\) phase (Synthesis phase): Nuclear DNA replication occurs, doubling the DNA content per cell (and centrosome duplication proceeds in the cytoplasm).
- \(\text{G}_2\) phase: Proteins required for mitosis are synthesized alongside continued cytoplasmic growth and final preparations for cell division.
- Metaphase of M-phase: Spindle fibres attach to kinetochores, and chromosomes align along the equatorial metaphase plate.

Step 3: Conclusion
The correct match is: (A)-(i), (B)-(ii), (C)-(iii), (D)-(iv).

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q177 - Basis of genetic mapping and DNA fingerprinting

questiontext.text: Which is the basis of genetic mapping of human genome as well as DNA finger printing ?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Genetic markers used for genome mapping and individual forensic identification depend on inherited, stable variations in nucleotide sequences across populations.

Step 2: Polymorphism in DNA Sequence
DNA sequence polymorphism arises due to non-lethal mutations accumulating in non-coding DNA over generations. Because these variations are stably inherited from parents to offspring, they provide the fundamental molecular basis for constructing genetic maps in the Human Genome Project as well as for forensic and paternity testing via DNA fingerprinting (using variable number tandem repeats or VNTRs).

Step 3: Conclusion
Polymorphism in DNA sequence forms the basis of both genetic mapping of the human genome and DNA fingerprinting.

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q178 - Maternal foetal incompatibility in erythroblastosis foetalis

questiontext.text: Which of the following conditions cause erythroblastosis foetalis ?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Erythroblastosis foetalis (hemolytic disease of the newborn) occurs due to an immunological Rh-incompatibility reaction between maternal blood and fetal erythrocytes.

Step 2: Pathophysiology of Rh Incompatibility
When an \(\text{Rh}^{-\text{ve}}\) mother carries an \(\text{Rh}^{+\text{ve}}\) fetus, maternal exposure to fetal \(\text{Rh}\) antigens during parturition stimulates maternal B cells to synthesize anti-\(\text{Rh}\) antibodies. In subsequent pregnancies with an \(\text{Rh}^{+\text{ve}}\) fetus, maternal \(\text{IgG}\) anti-\(\text{Rh}\) antibodies cross the placenta into the fetal circulation, lysing fetal erythrocytes and resulting in severe hemolytic anemia, jaundice, and potential fetal demise.

Step 3: Conclusion
Erythroblastosis foetalis is caused by the condition of Mother \(\text{Rh}^{-\text{ve}}\) and foetus \(\text{Rh}^{+\text{ve}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_2020_MCQ_Q179 - Chordate and vertebrate relationship justification

questiontext.text: All vertebrates are chordates but all chordates are not vertebrates, why ?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Phylum Chordata comprises three subphyla: Urochordata (Tunicata), Cephalochordata, and Vertebrata (Craniata). The presence of a notochord at some developmental stage is the unifying characteristic of all chordates.

Step 2: Distinction Between Chordates and Vertebrates
In subphylum Vertebrata, the embryonic notochord is replaced during development by a cartilaginous or bony vertebral column in the adult. In contrast, in protochordates (Urochordata and Cephalochordata), a vertebral column is never formed: urochordates possess a notochord restricted to the larval tail, and cephalochordates retain a persistent notochord extending from head to tail throughout life. Hence, while all vertebrates belong to phylum Chordata, chordates lacking a vertebral column are not vertebrates.

Step 3: Conclusion
All vertebrates are chordates but all chordates are not vertebrates because the notochord is replaced by a vertebral column in the adult of some chordates.
